articles.title: Ukraine energy company says its facilities seriously damaged after 13 Russian strikes in a week
articles.body:
Ukraine energy company says its facilities seriously damaged after 13 Russian strikes in a week
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia attacked facilities of Ukraine’s Naftogaz Group 13 times over the past week and has targeted its premises almost 300 times since the start of the year, the state energy company said Monday.
Russia has repeatedly battered the Ukrainian power grid since its all-out invasion more than four years ago. Moscow hopes to sap Ukraine’s will to fight by denying civilians light, heating and running water during the bitter winter months.
Ukrainian officials, who say Russia is “weaponizing winter,” fear Moscow will pursue its campaign through the coming winter, too.
Russian drones and missiles struck facilities in several regions of the country, with one asset hit multiple times during the week, Naftogaz said, reporting serious damage to equipment and production capacity. No employees were hurt in the attacks, the company said.
DTEK Group, a coal mining and power production company which says it is the largest private investor in Ukraine’s energy sector, also said a Russian attack started a fire at one of its mines, killing a 52-year-old man.
With troops largely bogged down by drones and robots along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line, both Russia and Ukraine are expanding their aerial campaigns and devising new long-range weapons.
Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia killed seven people, while five civilians died in Ukraine after strikes by Moscow’s forces, officials said Monday as they collated overnight attacks.
With the Russian capital now within range of Ukrainian drones that regularly attack the region, organizers canceled a large military music festival due to be held on central Moscow’s Red Square from Friday.
The organizers of the Spasskaya Tower International Military Music Festival said on social media Monday that the event was postponed until next year due to reasons beyond their control.
In May, authorities significantly scaled back Russia’s annual Victory Day celebrations on Red Square for the first time in nearly two decades. Officials put the move down to the “current operational situation” but did not elaborate.
Ukraine depended heavily on foreign military aid after Russia’s full-scale invasion of February 2022 but has gradually increased its domestically produced firepower, firing a salvo of more than 800 long-range drones at Russia on Sunday.
Ukraine also has successfully targeted depots owned by Wildberries, Russia’s main online retailer, as far as 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) from Ukraine’s border.
Russian forces have increasingly hit apartment blocks, ports, schools and hospitals, among other urban targets, killing close to 17,000 civilians, according to the United Nations. The death toll of 437 Ukrainian civilians in July was 70% higher than the same month in 2025, it said last week, as Russia’s barrages intensified.
Russia has exploited Ukraine’s severe shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, which are the only way of countering ballistic missiles.
But Kyiv is swiftly innovating, with Ukraine now developing its own ballistic missile to hit back at Russia and working with European countries on developing more anti-ballistic air defenses.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

articles.title: NATO no longer deters Russia. A new coalition could
articles.body:
Russia will keep escalating until Europe shows both the political will and the military capability to stop it, argues Hans Petter Midttun—and NATO can no longer supply either. In an interview with the Guildhall news agency, the former defense attaché to Ukraine makes the case for the Ukraine-anchored coalition he has argued for since long before this interview: Northern Europe together with Ukraine, credible from the day it is declared.
This interview was conducted in Russian by the Guildhall news agency and is republished here in an edited English translation. The subheadings are Euromaidan Press's.
Hans Petter Midttun is a non-resident research fellow at the Centre for Defence Strategies and a former defense attaché to Ukraine.
Why NATO no longer deters Russia
It seems that despite everything the West has done to deter Russia, the Russian threat to the West—particularly to the Baltic states and NATO members in general—is only increasing. What is your diagnosis? Why has the Western deterrence strategy failed, if you agree that it has?
Yes, I absolutely agree, and I have been saying this for quite some time.
To begin with, it is worth questioning your basic formulation—"the West." I have often used the term myself. Almost every time I write about what is happening, I use it. But recently I have begun to question whether it is still accurate.
If we regard the West as a civilization, as a strategic space, then we understand what we are talking about. Usually that means NATO and the European Union. But if we regard it as a political actor, as an entity responsible for deterrence, the situation becomes much more complicated.
For some time now I have questioned the viability of NATO. I am an officer myself, and I have been oriented toward NATO throughout my career. I have always believed in the Alliance. Almost everything I have done over nearly 40 years has been based on NATO doctrine, strategy, and tactics. But since 2022, I have seriously begun to question it. I have written publicly that I doubt the Alliance can survive in its current form. And I have said very clearly that it no longer deters Russia. I can prove it.
Please do.
There are three reasons I have pointed to repeatedly.
The first and most fundamental: if NATO were genuinely deterring Russia, Russia would never have invaded Ukraine. To most people that probably sounds strange, because under NATO's 2010 Strategic Concept, still in force in 2022, NATO was not obliged to defend Ukraine and had not declared any intention to. There was no commitment to Ukraine as such.
But the Strategic Concept stated clearly, under its second core task—crisis management—that in the event of a conflict threatening the security of the Alliance, NATO would use a combination of political and military instruments to manage and resolve it. What is happening in Ukraine is precisely such a conflict. It threatens the security of the Alliance, and the Alliance recognized this many years ago. So before the invasion, Russia must have looked at NATO and concluded it would not act.
The second point: if Russia were deterred, it would not be waging a constantly escalating hybrid war on NATO territory. It is already waging one. And, shamefully, NATO has not even acknowledged the fact. It talks in general terms, but it never calls what is happening what it is: a hybrid war, a campaign to undermine the Alliance. We are not acting on the basis of that reality.
The third point: if Russia were deterred, it would not now be preparing for a potential attack on NATO members.
So there are three very clear indicators that, whatever NATO believes about its own deterrence, Russia does not believe it. And that is what determines whether deterrence works. Deterrence is not determined in Washington or Brussels. It is determined in the Kremlin.
Why the answer cannot come from NATO
We still need to deter Russia from expanding its aggression further, including directly against NATO, which the Kremlin clearly regards as one possible scenario. How should the deterrence strategy be adjusted? What mechanisms need to be created?
Let me take one step back first, because I think it matters. I would argue this cannot be achieved through NATO. NATO will never be able to deter Russia. I would go further: NATO is no longer the solution. It has become part of the problem.
There are several reasons. During the Cold War, NATO took the risk of strategic miscalculation extremely seriously. If the Soviet Union provoked us—by sending a combat aircraft, a warship, or moving ground forces in our direction—NATO always responded. This was done to leave no room for miscalculation and no impression of local weaknesses the Soviet Union could exploit.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, we stopped acting this way—despite the fact that, for roughly 15 years before the full-scale war, Russia was challenging us, testing us, and doing many of the things the Soviet Union once did. We lost our credibility.
On top of that, a transatlantic divide has opened—a rupture between Europe and the United States. We see an America that is no longer a reliable ally but is becoming more of a strategic opponent. America treats the European Union as an opponent, and that creates an entirely different strategic environment. We are talking about a former ally that threatens to seize NATO territory—Greenland—and talks about annexing Canada. All of it opens a window of opportunity for Russia that it could previously only have dreamed of.
Part of the responsibility lies with Europe too, because we did not take security and defense seriously enough. We did not invest. We are now extremely vulnerable, with critical weaknesses that can be exploited. So we are in a moment of weakness, and Russia understands it. Russia also understands that this window is limited in time, and that is precisely what raises the risk of more serious developments.
The coalition, and which countries would form it
I appreciate the deeper assessment, but that is still diagnosis. What is the treatment? What concrete steps need to be taken, and by whom, to deter Russia again?
I spent so long on the previous question because I wanted to completely destroy the notion that NATO will be the solution. It will not. That means we have to look for something else.
We need some of the qualities NATO had in the 1980s. At the height of the Cold War, the member states—there were 16 then—knew who the adversary was. They all saw it the same way. They understood its strategic goals, its doctrine, its capabilities, its theater of operations. So every state was committed to countering the threat. We invested in defense—Europe spent roughly 3.8 percent of GDP on it—and we had a common strategy. In a sense we were a coalition of the like-minded. That is what I advocate rebuilding.
Trending Now
But it also means that, initially, a significant share of NATO members, and possibly some EU members, would have to remain outside such a structure. If you want a structure built on a common understanding of the threat and unity of purpose, you have to accept that not all states share the same aspirations. That is why I have named a number of countries that should become its founding members, with the ultimate goal of including all of Europe. But we start with a group of the like-minded.
Which countries do you have in mind?
My argument begins here, and it is one of the reasons the coalition is necessary: Ukraine will never become a member of NATO. To be honest, that was already clear five, four, and three years ago. It is a shameful situation. But that is exactly the point. Europe needs strategic autonomy. We have to stand on our own feet and defend Europe ourselves. We can no longer rely on the United States, so we need to build something else.
I believe this coalition should be built around Ukraine and the NB8 countries—the Nordic-Baltic Eight—together with the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Poland, and the Netherlands. Essentially, Northern Europe together with Ukraine. That configuration alone already creates enormous credibility. It would bring together not only Ukraine's battle-hardened armed forces—the Ground Forces, National Guard, Special Operations Forces, air defense, and Unmanned Systems Forces—but also high-tech European air forces, navies, and special operations forces. Almost immediately you have a structure with real credibility, because we share common values and a common understanding of how to fight Russia and how to defeat it. Simply announcing such a coalition would have a deterrent effect.
What you are saying resonates with me. But the Russian threat exists here and now. Building full European strategic autonomy without the United States would take at least five years. What do we do in the meantime? How do we deter Russia now?
I would challenge that. I have heard the argument many times. We are not talking about forces that exist only on paper. The armed forces of the countries I named already exist today, and they are built on the same standards—NATO standards. We do not need to invent new ones. They share a doctrinal foundation and, in many respects, similar strategic approaches. We can use NATO technologies, standards, documents, doctrines, and research—everything the Alliance has already created is available to us. And Ukraine is already largely NATO-compatible. Will such a coalition be as effective today as it could be in five years? No. But Ukraine itself was not as effective five years ago as it is today.
The nuclear question
What about nuclear weapons? Full deterrence of Russia is hard to imagine without a nuclear component.
I would challenge that too. We have all grown accustomed to relying on the idea of nuclear deterrence. I am not saying it does not matter, and some of the states I named do possess a nuclear capability.
But not comparable to Russia's arsenal.
Yes, but it does not quite work that way, and that is the point. Both Russia and the United States have lost wars without using nuclear weapons. The consequences of using them are so catastrophic that the great powers—including China—regard the threshold as extremely high. You could argue Russia might not have attacked Ukraine if Ukraine had kept nuclear weapons. Possibly. But that is in the past. The war is already under way, and after years of it—after Ukraine has crossed practically every one of Russia's so-called red lines—Russia still has not used nuclear weapons against Ukraine.
So we cannot abandon the idea of a coalition simply because it lacks an arsenal comparable to Russia's. On the contrary: we have to recognize that the threshold for use is so high that the probability of actual use is extremely low. Not zero, but extremely low. And we are no longer talking only about deterring Russia. Russia is already at war with Europe and waging war on Ukraine. We are talking about how to end that war, with the tools we have. We cannot do it through NATO. We cannot rely on the United States to do it for us. So either we build something genuinely credible, or we accept that Russia will keep acting against us.
Why it starts with a declaration
You said the cost of using nuclear weapons must be unacceptable to Russia. The same logic can apply to the conventional threat. What concrete steps can we take now to make the cost of further conventional aggression unacceptable to the Kremlin?
The solution is right in front of us. The starting point is what Ukraine itself has said many times: Russia will escalate for as long as we let it, and it responds to nothing but strength. So until we—the West, or the coalition, whichever term you prefer—stand up and demonstrate both the political will and the military capability to act, Russia will keep escalating.
That is why, when you asked about the timeline, I said: if these countries had united yesterday, today, or tomorrow and announced the creation of such a coalition and their intention to fight together, that alone would completely change Russia's strategic assessment.
Today Russia is fighting one country, Ukraine, supported by around 50 partner states. But it is still fighting only one country. If that declaration were made tomorrow, the situation would change radically. Russia already finds it difficult to fight Ukraine; it would face a fundamentally different reality if Ukraine formally joined a coalition with European military powers.
So this is not only about physical capabilities. It is about changing Russia's perception of its strategic environment. And it starts with a declaration.
The next step would be the actual conduct of military operations, if necessary. But it begins with the declaration. That would completely change Russia's strategic calculus.

articles.title: Russia to Free Up Manpower by Replacing Border Troops With North Korean Soldiers, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Russia might free up troops from border regions to bolster intense frontline sectors by replacing them with North Korean troops, a Ukrainian military spokesperson said on Monday.
Serhiy Bratchuk, the spokesperson for the Ukrainian Volunteer Army, said on television that up to 20,000 “combat-ready” Russian troops on the border might be transferred to the “hottest destinations,” with their positions replaced by North Korean troops.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is quite likely that there are 15,000-20,000, perhaps even no more, combat-ready Russian fighters there, they will transfer them just like these reservists, respectively, from the territory of the Russian Federation to the hottest destinations,” Bratchuk said, as reported by state media Ukrinform.
“It is obvious that this attempt by the Kremlin to use these units is aimed at freeing exclusively Russian combat units that are currently in the Russian border area, transferring them to the relevant most active sections of the Russian-Ukrainian front,” he added.
“Well, actually, the North Koreans will replace them there.”
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in early August that North Korea plans to station between 30,000 and 50,000 troops in Russia, amid reports that Pyongyang has bolstered arms transfers, as well as potentially deploying ballistic missile launchers and personnel, to Russian regions bordering Ukraine.
While Zelensky has warned that Russia is eyeing a major mobilization in autumn 2026, after the September State Duma elections, to replenish its ranks amid high battlefield losses, Western reports suggest that Russia is currently delaying the move by relying on volunteers.
Russia Places Son of RFK Jr. on Wanted List for Fighting in Ukraine
Ukraine’s defense ministry estimated that Russia lost around 43,000 troops in July 2026, while the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) suggested in the same month that Russia recruited 1,070-1,090 troops per day on average, which fell short of the battlefield losses.
Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in June 2024, with Pyongyang deploying troops to Russia’s Kursk region in October the same year to help Moscow recapture lost territories.
While both initially denied reports of North Korean troop deployments, they later acknowledged them in April 2025.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Drones Are Changing the Air War, Ukraine Racing to Respond
articles.body:
Russia is increasingly turning to jet-powered and missile drones as it seeks to overcome Ukrainian air defenses, with newer versions of the Geran and Banderol systems posing a faster and potentially more difficult-to-intercept threat.
The shift was examined by RBC-Ukraine on Monday, which spoke with military experts about Russia’s growing use of jet drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, Russia is increasingly relying on faster drones as the effectiveness of conventional Shaheds in large-scale attacks declines.
“The Russians are increasingly establishing mass production of jet drones and missile drones and are increasingly using them to strike the territory of Ukraine,” Zemlyanyi said, according to RBC-Ukraine.
The key advantage is speed. Faster drones give Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and destroy them, potentially allowing more targets to penetrate defensive layers and reach areas farther from the frontline.
A new class between drones and missiles
The emerging Russian systems are set to include new Geran modifications as well as Banderol missile drones.
However, military expert Oleh Katkov, editor-in-chief of Defense Express, said that the term “jet drone” increasingly covers weapons with significantly different characteristics.
Some newer Geran variants, including the Geran-4 and Geran-5, are approaching cruise missiles in terms of their design and capabilities, he said.
Ukraine Says Russian Explosives Plant Hit, Two Workshops Destroyed
This makes the distinction increasingly important for air defense planners: weapons that are faster than conventional Shaheds but cheaper and potentially easier to produce than cruise missiles could give Russia another way to conduct large-scale strikes.
However, jet drones are also considerably more difficult to manufacture at scale. Their main bottleneck is the jet engine, which is more expensive and technologically complex than the engines used in conventional Shaheds.
Katkov said Russia’s ability to expand production depends heavily on how many engines it can obtain from Chinese private companies.
Russia could eventually attempt to reproduce the approach it used with Shahed-type drones: initially importing components before developing domestic production and simplifying designs for mass manufacturing.
Composite materials and other components also pose production challenges, according to Zemlyanyi.
The greater speed of the new drones creates another problem for Ukraine: the economics of interception. Systems such as Patriot, SAMP/T, and IRIS-T can engage high-speed aerial targets, but using expensive surface-to-air missiles against relatively inexpensive drones is often economically inefficient.
That is driving interest in cheaper interceptor drones, including systems similar to Ukraine’s P1-Sun. Ukraine is developing new interceptor models, although their ability to reliably engage the fastest Russian targets remains a key question.
Other air defense systems, including Mistral, Skynex, and Gepard, can also be used against some high-speed targets, depending on their characteristics.
Ukraine is developing its own jet drones
Ukraine is not simply reacting to the Russian shift. According to Zemlyanyi, Ukrainian developers began working on jet-powered drones before Russia, with systems including Bars and Palyanytsya already being used for long-range strikes.
Ukrainian jet drones have been employed against military and strategic targets in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia.
However, speed comes with trade-offs. More sophisticated engines and designs increase production costs, while a larger engine can limit the warhead that a drone can carry.
For Ukraine, the challenge is therefore to balance speed, range, payload, and cost rather than simply develop the fastest possible drone.
Will jet drones replace Shaheds or cruise missiles?
Experts cited by RBC-Ukraine do not expect jet drones to completely replace either conventional Shaheds or cruise missiles.
Jet drones can be faster and potentially cheaper than cruise missiles, but they remain technologically inferior to missiles in areas such as navigation, electronics, protection systems, and warhead capabilities, Zemlyanyi said.
Instead, they are emerging as an intermediate category between conventional long-range attack drones and cruise missiles.
For Russia, their main attraction is the possibility of combining greater speed with mass attacks. For Ukraine, the answer will likely involve a combination of improved air defenses, cheaper interceptor drones, and its own growing fleet of high-speed long-range weapons.
The result is unlikely to be the disappearance of Shaheds or cruise missiles.

articles.title: CNN gets rare look at Ukraine’s empty Patriot system
articles.body:
- CNN gained rare access to a Ukrainian Patriot battery that has not fired in six weeks due to a shortage of interceptor missiles.
- Zelensky said Ukraine has access to only 1 percent of the U.S. Patriot stockpile despite needing 5 percent to survive the winter.
A Patriot air defense battery inside Ukraine has sat with empty launch tubes for weeks, its crew unable to fire because the country has nearly exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles, CNN reported after gaining rare access to the system.
CNN was the first outlet allowed to visit an operational Patriot unit on Ukrainian territory, agreeing not to disclose the system’s model or location. The battery’s chief engineer, identified only by his first name, Dmytro, for security reasons, told CNN he had not seen the launcher fire in six weeks. The first time his unit ran out of interceptors entirely was in December 2025.
“This is a really heartbreaking sight when you have equipment but you’re not able to intercept any missile,” Dmytro said. “Ballistic missiles are flying over your head and you are not able to do anything with it, and behind you, there are civilians.”
President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN Ukraine needs 5 percent of the U.S. Patriot stockpile to survive the winter but currently has access to only 1 percent. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since May 2022, driven by a sustained rise in Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A separate report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that U.S. stocks of Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors have fallen from more than 2,300 before the war between Israel and Iran began in June to roughly 800, with THAAD interceptor inventories nearly halved. Coalition forces defending against Iranian missiles used an average of 225 interceptors per day during the first four days of that conflict, according to the Foreign Policy Research Institute, against a Lockheed Martin production rate of 620 PAC-3 interceptors for all of 2025, or about 1.7 per day.
The Pentagon signed a seven-year deal with Lockheed Martin in January to raise annual PAC-3 production to 2,000 missiles by 2030.
Zelensky told CNN he has offered Raytheon and Lockheed Martin full ownership and control of any interceptor manufacturing plant the companies would permit inside Ukraine.
“It will be your company,” Zelensky recalled telling the manufacturers. “It will be our brains, our hands, our engineers. And I will do my best to build the great company… for them. Because I don’t need to sell [the interceptors] to anybody else. I need for my country.”
At the NATO summit in Ankara in June, President Trump offered Ukraine licenses to begin manufacturing Patriot interceptors domestically. Representatives from Raytheon and Lockheed Martin subsequently traveled to Kyiv to meet with Zelensky, but Trump later expressed doubts that the licensing arrangement would proceed. A White House official told CNN no decisions had been made or guarantees given on Patriot interceptor production, citing the priority of protecting U.S. technology.
“I want to get it,” Zelensky said. “I think his word is the word of president of the United States. And I hope that I will get it.”
Asked by CNN whether Ukraine could build a Patriot battery and interceptor immediately if intellectual property restrictions were set aside, Dmytro said it could not. “This is a very complex procedure, and it requires a lot of knowledge, a lot of technical information,” he said.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point has separately been developing the FP-7.x, a lower-cost interceptor under its FREYJA air and missile defense project, intended to reduce reliance on imported PAC-3 missiles. The system has undergone controlled flight testing but has not yet demonstrated repeated ballistic missile interceptions in the way the operationally established PAC-3 has.

articles.title: Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
articles.body:
Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Any projections about Ukraine's postwar politics should start with the recognition that Russia's ongoing war has taken the country into unknown territory.[1] It is possible to say that the war's scope and scale have had a social impact in Ukraine that can be compared only to that of a revolution. The war has dismantled the old social contract between the ruling elites and the people. Moreover, it has reshaped, if not redefined, the fundamentals of Ukrainian statehood. The war revealed the central role of civil society (including volunteer movements, grassroots mobilization, independent media, and influencers), exposed the strengths and weaknesses of state institutions and the legal system, and forced the Armed Forces and security services to adapt rapidly. However, to borrow Alexis de Tocqueville's phrase, no matter how profound the revolution, the new order inherits important traits and patterns of the old one.
The Long Shadow of Corruption
Populism and corruption have been formidable impediments to the economic and political development of independent Ukraine. In November 2020, the editorial board of the Financial Times opined on the constitutional and legal challenges facing President Volodymyr Zelensky in achieving his stated goal of dismantling the oligarchic state capture that had characterized Ukraine's political and economic system since independence in 1991. It expressed concerns that Zelensky, whom it called "a textbook populist," wanted to avoid an uphill struggle in tackling the roots of the problem, instead preferring quick solutions that enjoyed broad public approval.
After Zelensky was elected in 2019, he succeeded in converting his wide popular support into unprecedented control of the legislative and executive branches of government. During the first eighteen months of his presidency, terms such as "turbo regime" and "deoligarchization" reflected his almost unlimited power and the steamroller-like process he used to push new laws through parliament. He and his allies argued this was necessary to "reset" the political system and rid the country of entrenched oligarchic influence and high-level corruption.
However, it soon became apparent that members of Zelensky's entourage had taken over the existing schemes of illegal personal enrichment, even after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. Since then, key figures of the executive have been investigated for corruption, including: the head of the Office of the President Andriy Yermak; three of his deputies (Oleg Tatarov, Rostyslav Shurma, and Kyrylo Tymoshenko); deputy prime minister Oleksii Chernyshov; former minister of defense and Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Rustem Umerov; minister of justice and of energy Herman Halushchenko; and head of the State Property Fund of Ukraine, Dmytro Sennychenko. Some of the figures who faced charges—including Shurma, Sennychenko, and Timur Mindich, a businessman and the president's close friend—left the country days or hours before arrest warrants were issued, which infuriated the public because it showed that powerful figures could violate strict wartime border controls and had access to privileged information about investigations.
In addition, as of December 2025, fifteen members of parliament from Zelensky's Servant of the People party were being investigated for corruption, with some facing accusations of buying the votes of their colleagues. In January 2026, former prime minister Yuliya Tymoshenko, who leads a parliamentary faction that has aligned itself with Servant of the People, was caught red-handed by the National Anticorruption Bureau as she offered bribes to secure the votes of fellow members of parliament.
Already in 2023, one of the authors warned that Ukraine was backsliding in its fight against corruption and that the public would blame Zelensky and the government if the issue was not addressed. In a public opinion poll that year, 78 percent of respondents said that Zelensky was directly responsible for fighting corruption in the government and the military. Even though Ukrainians saw him as a national symbol of resistance against Russia, the implications of high-level corruption scandals were clear at the time: Unless the president took action against accused top members of his administration, perceptions of impunity risked undermining trust in him and damaging society's cohesion and will to resist the invasion.
The situation has grown worse since then. In a September 2025 poll, 71 percent of respondents—including 62 percent of those who said they trusted Zelensky—said that corruption had increased during the full-scale invasion. In an April 2026 poll, 54 percent of respondents said that corruption was a greater threat than military aggression, compared to only 39 percent who said the opposite.
These figures suggest that most Ukrainians see high-level corruption as a form of state treason and a threat to statehood. There is strong evidence that Zelensky, earlier in his presidency, was sensitive to such public attitudes; in 2023, for example, he publicly expressed a positive opinion about amending legislation to make the punishment for high-level corruption equivalent to that of state treason, which is a life sentence in most cases.
However, by 2025 popular outrage over corruption had turned against Zelensky. The clearest evidence of public anger about high-level corruption was the "cardboard Maidan" in July 2025—the wave of peaceful student protests against Zelensky's moves to curtail the powers and reduce the independence of anticorruption institutions in order to shield his allies from criminal investigation, including his longtime friend Mindich. It was a powerful reminder of the mass protests in 2004 and 2014 and showed that Ukrainians were willing to defy martial law,[2] which limits the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, in order to pressure the president on corruption.
Decentralized Resilience
Amid the invasion and malfunctioning state institutions, powerful civic activism, modern entrepreneurship, and the experience of decades of those who studied in the West went a long way toward enabling the national struggle for survival. Ukrainians' long tradition of solving problems in a decentralized manner when the central government was unwilling or unable proved critical to the country's resilience. Mayors and volunteers independently built ties with military units and used their resources to procure necessary lethal and nonlethal equipment needed on the front. Nongovernmental charity foundations like the Serhiy Prytula Foundation, the Come Back Alive Foundation, and the Sternenko Community led the way in providing millions of strike and reconnaissance drones, interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems, and access to commercial satellite imagery. These grassroots initiatives more than supplemented the state's resource-constrained and bureaucratically burdened efforts.
Moreover, the agility and adaptability of the defense forces were key factors that allowed Ukraine to survive in the initial phases of the full-scale war. This was the result of decentralized and self-organized networks of cooperation across broader sections of society. Just like community leaders and civic volunteers, the Army and National Guard brigades that turned out to be the most effective did not wait for plans to be introduced from the top. Rather, they independently established their own unmanned systems units, supply chains, research and development laboratories, medical infrastructure, training programs, and public-relations infrastructure.
These innovative practices reflect profound long-term shifts in the attitudes of Ukrainians, who have developed new expectations toward private initiative and state intervention, and have grown even more skeptical of relying on welfare provided by the government. This portends major shifts in postwar politics. Ukrainians will almost certainly continue to trust decentralized but well-connected networks of professionals at the national and regional levels more than they trust central government institutions or legacy political parties. Officers, volunteers, and entrepreneurs who made a difference during the war will have strong credentials for postwar leadership roles. Intense clashes are likely to emerge between wartime leaders and political figures viewed as products of the corrupt "old system." The victors in this competition will be those capable of mass mobilization through appeals to national security and justice, and who can build efficient nationwide political machines.
Zelensky's decision in mid-July to fire Mykhailo Fedorov, the tech-savvy minister of defense who is well-connected with top Western defense companies, illustrates this "clash of generations" in Ukrainian politics and governance. In his farewell statement, Fedorov outlined what he sees as major deficiencies in the "old way" of running the army and country during wartime. If Zelensky does not find a way to mend fences, Fedorov's dismissal might prove to be a watershed moment for old and new elites to consolidate and prepare for a postwar power struggle.
Moderates Versus Radicals
After the war, Ukraine will face the dual challenge of rebuilding while deterring new threats from Russia. The role of the state in recovery and development will grow significantly. This will require strengthening independent oversight and institutional checks and balances. It may also raise the issue of guaranteeing the welfare of all those working in the security and defense sector.
The public will expect the state to assist and support veterans, the relatives of fallen servicemen and civilians, former prisoners of war and deportees returning from Russia, and citizens who lost their homes and property because of hostilities. Debates over the extent to which the Ukrainian state should seek to hold Russian officials accountable for war crimes (if the international community fails to do so) and punish collaborators for their misdeeds are also likely to dominate the political landscape. Inevitably, there will be a national debate about the responsibility of Zelensky and the government for decisions made—or not made—before and during the war. Ukrainians will also demand close scrutiny of the activities of those who controlled politics and the economy before the invasion. These debates are likely to divide political actors and citizens into camps of "moderates" and "radicals," depending on whether they demand symbolic or uncompromising justice on key issues, and whether they favor selective or equal approaches to different actors and social groups.
The moderates camp will probably try to shift the focus away from immediate justice toward building a stronger state that is capable of protecting Ukraine and preventing a new attack. Figures such as Fedorov and Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, who have consistently called for national unity and looked to the future rather than focusing on the past, might emerge as leaders of this camp. Moderates will try to direct public anger against Russia while seeking to defuse internal feuds. They will call for an acceleration of reforms necessary for joining the EU—which they will argue is the ultimate prize for postwar Ukraine and future generations. This camp will support special and "black" operations inside Russia and other countries to bring war criminals and traitors to justice.
Mobilization will be another issue that will divide Ukrainians after the war. Many thousands of men paid bribes to leave the country during the war or escaped mobilization by securing, through any means, exemptions from military service. At the same time, military commissions drafted thousands of unfit men, including with physical and mental disabilities, into service. These men cannot fight, but they also cannot be released from service until the end of the war, burdening the military and inflating the number of troops.
To address Ukraine's human-resources challenges, the moderate camp will probably call for the return of Ukrainians from abroad or argue in favor of migration from Africa, Asia, or Latin America to fill labor shortages. Moreover, to decrease public tensions over mobilization, moderates will argue in favor of increasing immigration and enrolling more foreigners in the ranks of the Armed Forces. (For instance, before his dismissal Fedorov was preparing a plan to substitute up to 50 percent of assault troops with contracted foreigners.) The idea is that such measures would encourage young Ukrainians not to leave the country because of the risk of being drafted to the frontline. In addition, Budanov has spoken out against mobilizing young Ukrainians, which in his view would threaten to eliminate an "entire generation."
However, the moderates will face a serious political dilemma. It will be hard to convince millions of refugees to return without strong security guarantees and economic stability, but it will be impossible to maintain a capable army and economic development in a situation of severe deficits of human resources.
The radicals will claim that any dilution of justice will lay the groundwork for another national disaster and a new Russian invasion. Their arguments may resemble those made in the early 1990s and in 2014, when certain political actors argued that all remnants of the old regime—whether former communists or collaborators of president Viktor Yanukovych and his Party of Regions—needed to be purged.
Several public figures with significant political and social influence—in the form of large followership in social media, the permanent attention of traditional media to what they say or do, and evident political ambitions—have the potential to become leaders of the radical camp. They are Serhiy Sternenko, a prominent volunteer and vocal opponent of Zelensky since 2021; Bohdan "Tavr" Krotevych, ex–chief of staff of the Azov Brigade; and Yuriy Butusov, former editor-in-chief of the Censor.net news portal and a drone company commander in the Khartiia Brigade. All three have attacked Zelensky for what they argue were poorly conceived and implemented decisions before and after the full-scale invasion.
Moreover, the radicals will call for the prosecution of political, administrative, and military leaders whose decisions contributed to Ukraine's devastation and huge human losses. Figures in this camp have already begun to criticize what they see as reckless, politically driven decisions that have cost the lives of thousands of the country's defenders with no operational or even tactical benefit on the battlefield. They have stressed the need for independent investigations of pointless offensive operations led by the assault regiments commanded by protégés of General Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom Zelensky removed as commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces in late July in response to public protests. They have also pointed out the absence of relevant basic military training for the majority of recruits in the Army. The public reaction to a recent independent investigation that uncovered the suspicious deaths of twenty-five recruits in the 425th Assault Regiment "Skelya" shows how sensitive and explosive this issue will become after the war.
Several whistleblowers, including decorated officers like ex-battalion commander of 46th Airborne Assault Brigade Colonel Anatoliy Kozel (Kupol), Major Oleksandr Shyrshyn from the elite 47th Mechanized Brigade, and ex-commander of 58th Mechanized Brigade Colonel Dmytro Kashchenko, have at different times warned about these and other critical shortcomings among senior political and military commanders. In April 2026, Colonel Roman Chervinskyi of the Security Service publicly accused Budanov of abusing power during the war.
These developments are alarming signs that after the war radicalized veterans and civic activists are going to shape the national agenda by saying that Zelensky and the executive failed to provide justice and security during the war. They will have a strong case to make if they can draw on the vivid memories of hardship felt by ordinary soldiers and their families.
Moreover, Zelensky himself has played a part in creating moderate and radical contenders. His dismissals of General Valeriy Zaluzhny from the position of commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in 2024 and Fedorov in July were reminiscent of politics under former president Leonid Kuchma (1994–2004). Kuchma prosecuted moderate deputy prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko in 2000 and fired moderate prime minister Viktor Yushchenko in 2001. Both later came together to unite opposition forces and challenge Kuchma's regime during the election cycles of 2002–2004, culminating in the Orange Revolution and end of Kuchma's rule.
New Nationalism and Grassroots Structures
Two factors will determine whether the moderates or radicals win the support of the public and the postwar competition for power.
First, to be successful, political leaders and organizations will have to show that they embrace and practice a modern, sophisticated version of Ukrainian nationalism. The war proved to most Ukrainians that the nationalist political parties and groups who consistently warned about Russian threats and subversion in the fields of popular culture, education, and the economy had a point. The mainstream political establishment is already increasingly adopting elements of nationalistic ideology in its rhetoric. For instance, Zelensky in January 2026 issued an order to establish a "national pantheon" to commemorate the heroes of the fight for independence in the twentieth century, including leaders of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). In May, he announced the reburial of one of the OUN's leaders, Andriy Melnyk, and issued a decree renaming a unit of the special operations forces after the "heroes of the UPA." These decisions sparked a diplomatic crisis with Poland, which blames the OUN and UPA for Second World War atrocities against ethnic Poles. Many Ukrainians, however, see these organizations as having fought for Ukraine's independence against the Soviet Union, as well as against Nazi Germany.
At the same time, as one of the authors argued in 2022, Ukrainian nationalism has been transforming into a nonpartisan, inclusive civic ideology that is embraced by the majority. In a poll in March 2023, 65 and 47 percent of respondents, respectively, said they thought that new public figures such as Zelensky and Zaluzhny had played key roles in defending the country, demonstrating that Ukrainians see these two men as nation-building figures amid the horrors of war. In another 2023 poll, 42 percent named Zaluzhny as a symbol of Ukraine, second only to the poet Taras Shevchenko (56 percent). With 31 percent, Zelensky was ahead of the Second World War radical leader Stepan Bandera (27 percent), seventeenth-century Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky (26 percent), and Vyacheslav Chornovil, one of the leaders of the independence movement in the late Soviet period (26 percent).
The second factor is the importance of grassroots structures. Ukrainians have come to recognize the role of local communities, civic activists, and decentralized structures—especially military units—in building national identity. Popular units and leaders within them such as the Azov Brigade (Denys Prokopenko), the 3rd Assault Brigade (Andriy Biletsky), and the Khartiia Brigade (Oleh Kozhemyako) may become umbrella organizations for political movements. (Although its early roots were in far-right ideologies, Azov has the reputation of one of the most capable fighting units and one that cares about the lives of ordinary soldiers. It attracts volunteers from different age groups and gender, ethnic, and language backgrounds. Its commanders rarely take sides in political clashes.)
In sum, individuals who demonstrated leadership during the war and achieved military, technological, administrative, diplomatic, or humanitarian success will find themselves at the forefront of political competition after the war. The most successful postwar political forces will have strong national leaders with solid wartime credentials while relying on horizontal structures that emerged during the war, including volunteer networks, veterans groups, and informal associations of local community leaders.
In Search of a Unifying Figure
Amid public concerns over corruption and lingering questions about his wartime decisions, Zelensky's window of opportunity to be a national unifying figure has probably closed. But his political networks will give him a considerable opportunity to retain influence if he leaves office. Prior to his arrest in May 2026, Yermak—until then his closest aide—had launched a project to forge a coalition of military commanders, veterans, and volunteers with the goal of creating a new political force that could contest postwar elections under Zelensky's leadership. Since Yermak's arrest, Zelensky has continued this project on his own.
Zelensky has paid more attention to his standing and reputation among the military since he sacked Yermak in November 2025. Since the beginning of this year, he has participated in eight meetings with service members from various branches of the Armed Forces, suggesting that he is investing time and effort to rebuild support among veterans as a way to maintain political influence, whether he decides to run for another term or not.
On the other hand, former commander-in-chief Zaluzhny, now the ambassador to the United Kingdom, has emerged in the public consciousness as a strong contender for the presidency even though he has not yet declared his ambitions to run for office. He is a unique figure and is trusted both by moderates, who laud him for leading and modernizing the Armed Forces, and by radicals, who believe he is too strong to be subdued or corrupted by shadowy politics. At the same time, Zaluzhny is a political novice, and his knowledge of English and understanding of the economy, in particular, are significant shortcomings. He will have to prove to Ukrainians that he has the qualities to lead the country on the international stage through a turbulent postwar future.
Someone else may still yet emerge as a unifying figure. Ukraine needs its next leader not only to focus on healing a wounded nation, defending against Russian threats, and modernizing the economy, but also to unite political forces: If the first postwar president is accepted by moderates but not trusted by radicals, there is a high risk of dangerous civil division that will undermine medium- to long-term stability.
The Tough Task Ahead
On many occasions throughout its contemporary history, Ukraine has witnessed the emergence of new faces and new political forces. However, few of them survived the test of parliamentary democracy, especially when it came to coalition-building. Many leaders focused on their personal ambitions and created weak party structures that rose and fell in parallel with their own fate. Stronger political actors have tended to concentrate, if not monopolize, power in their hands at the expense of junior partners, and in some cases they went so far as to prosecute the opposition. Moreover, external influence, especially from Russia, has repeatedly turned heated domestic political competition into an existential fight. These factors remain and will frame postwar politics. Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Considering how bitter internal feuds undermined Ukrainian statehood in the past, Ukraine's key power brokers—including Zelensky, Zaluzhny, Budanov, Biletsky, and Prokopenko—should reach an agreement so that free and fair elections can be held across the country and then negotiate some form of power-sharing. Since all of them have armed men and women behind them, maintaining calm and ensuring that the next electoral cycle can proceed without voter intimidation will be critical. Ukraine has already seen in 1918–1921 a period of otamanshchyna, when anarchy and bitter power struggles between rebel warlords contributed to Ukraine being subjugated by Russia under Bolshevik rule. This time, Ukrainians must find a way to avoid bringing violence into the political process. It is vital that postwar election results be accepted and that power be peacefully transferred to the winners.
Ukraine's postwar leaders will have to decide how to reconcile national priorities—especially spending on defense and social welfare—with the demands of major donors like the International Monetary Fund and the EU, including those regarding democratic rights and the rule of law. They will also need to adapt domestic policies to the permanent threat from Russia without returning to martial law and without concentrating power under the executive.
So long as Ukraine is not a member of NATO or the EU, its leaders will have to build an agile and innovative national security architecture based on defense alliances and arrangements with other democracies, not only in Europe but also in the Middle East (Israel) and the Asia-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines). Postwar Ukraine might also embark on trying to reshape its neighborhood. Ukrainians will have a hard time feeling secure with neighboring Belarus under the puppet regime of Aleksander Lukashenko and with Moldova's Transnistria region still a Russian-controlled enclave. Once the war ends, or even pauses, Ukraine's leaders are likely to address these threats, ideally in collaboration with the West but potentially unilaterally. They will need a more expansive and sophisticated view of engaging with countries in Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere. Its new leaders will need to maintain an equal focus on national defense and on securing the economic resources and trade relationships necessary to mitigate domestic demographic decline and fuel reconstruction.
These challenges will require the emerging crop of leaders to display a high degree of statesmanship. They must understand that personality-driven politics, polarization, legislative gridlock, and failure to respect the rule of law were profound mistakes that almost cost Ukraine its independence and statehood. If the country is to win the peace, it will need leaders who can break from the past once and for all.
Petro Burkovskyi, executive director of the Ilko Kucheriv Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Olexiy Haran, is a professor at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

articles.title: Russia Builds Drone Bases Near NATO, Putting Poland Within Reach
articles.body:
Russia has built a network of new drone launch sites near its borders with Belarus and Ukraine, potentially putting NATO territory within range of Moscow’s newest long-range attack drones.
Satellite images and leaked documents reviewed by The Telegraph identified at least 59 new launch rails across 10 Russian military and civilian sites. Some of the bases are already being used to launch attacks against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The expansion is raising concerns that the infrastructure could eventually be used to threaten NATO countries, including Poland.
New drone hubs near NATO
The launch sites include repurposed military bases and civilian airports, as well as newly built facilities carved out in remote areas of Russia.
Drone intelligence company DroneSec analyzed satellite imagery and found that around 20 of the new launch rails are long enough to accommodate Russia’s latest long-range drones.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The sites are also being expanded. At some locations, additional launch rails are under construction, suggesting Moscow is preparing to launch larger numbers of drones.
One base reportedly has enough storage capacity for more than 1,000 drones.
Seven of the 10 sites identified by The Telegraph have already been used in recent Russian attacks on Kyiv, according to open-source tracking data.
US Military YouTuber Paid His Own Way to Cover Ukraine's Front Line
                                                                                                                                                                         
Faster, longer-range drones
Russia has rapidly upgraded its version of the Iranian-designed Shahed drone, developing faster variants that can travel hundreds of miles and carry heavier warheads.
The newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones are reportedly capable of reaching speeds that make them harder for air defenses to intercept while carrying payloads of up to 90 kilograms, according to leaked Ukrainian government documents.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has also warned that Russia is experimenting with arming Geran drones with air-to-air missiles, potentially allowing them to target aircraft defending Ukrainian cities.
The drones are being supplied to the new launch hubs by Russian production facilities, including the Alabuga special economic zone, one of Moscow’s main drone manufacturing centers.
The expansion does not mean Russia is preparing to attack NATO immediately. But the new infrastructure gives Moscow more options if the Kremlin decides to escalate against the alliance.
Some of the sites could put Warsaw within range of Russia’s newest long-range attack drones.
European and US intelligence officials have warned that Russia could consider provocations against Poland, including attacks on critical infrastructure or false-flag operations designed to blame Ukraine.
NATO has said it is strengthening its ability to detect, operate and counter drones as the technology rapidly changes modern warfare.

articles.title: While Waiting for Patriots
articles.body:
“During the night, Ukrainian air defenses failed to shoot down a single Russian ballistic missile” – morning news reports like this are common. It seems we have nothing with which to counter Russia’s super-fast and extremely destructive weapons.
Only Patriot missiles are a match for them, and recently, when asked by journalists about the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, Trump said the US needed them for their own defense.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
So, we can be sure that the explosions we hear at night are not shots fired at missiles, but rather Russian missiles hitting their targets: warehouses, gas depots, or railway station platforms where passengers are gathered, waiting for their train.
Since the beginning of August, numerous large warehouses belonging to supermarkets, Ukrainian manufacturers, and retail chains that import building materials, white goods, and auto parts have suffered in this way. The list of affected companies is long.
The owners of the storage facilities dotted around our large cities know that if they haven’t already fallen victim to Russian missile attacks, they certainly will, and businesses are starting to restructure logistics.
Goods must be distributed immediately to stores, while any stockpiles are broken up and stored in smaller, less conspicuous facilities. This requires greater coordination, more gasoline, and more time. Supermarkets have warned that prices on some products will rise by at least 20 percent. The official explanation to customers for the impending price increase is succinct: “Due to Russia’s destruction of food products.”
US Military YouTuber Paid His Own Way to Cover Ukraine's Front Line
In the stores of the supermarket chain Novus, “out-of-stock” signs read: “This item is unavailable because it was destroyed by Russians.”
Ukraine’s largest online purchase platform, Rozetka, the equivalent of Russia’s Wildberries, was recently hit hard when a key warehouse and logistics center, on the outskirts of Kyiv, was destroyed.
At the same time, the private courier service Nova Poshta, which is often used to deliver Rozetka goods to customers, was also targeted by ballistic missiles. Customers who paid for their goods in advance are waiting to see if their purchases will arrive, while others are posting photos of their Nova Poshta parcel with a sticker reading: “Your parcel survived the fire.”
The other day, we stopped at an Epicenter hypermarket – a huge retail space for hardware, construction goods, and much else besides. In the event of an air raid warning, it would be impossible to evacuate such a store and find shelter within the five minutes it takes for a Russian ballistic missile to travel from its launch pad to its target.
While we were looking for a new axe and some drill bits, I automatically memorized the route to the exit, but I noticed that other shoppers were perfectly calm, despite several recent ballistic missile and drone strikes on other Epicenter hypermarkets.
Over the past few weeks, Russia has also destroyed Ukrainian warehouses containing newly printed books - more than 10 million copies. The destroyed volumes are mostly school textbooks, which are published under government contracts and are a vital source of revenue for several publishing houses. How will these lost textbooks be accounted for now? Who will pay for them? The publishing houses that fail to deliver to the Ministry of Education, or the state itself?
In any case, the destruction of book warehouses has pushed a number of well-known publishing houses to the brink of bankruptcy, including Ranok, which specializes in children’s books. The affected publishers will try to offset some of their losses by raising the price of new books. However, the margin for increase is small because prices have already risen beyond what is psychologically acceptable for most buyers, and book sales are falling.
Two of the three Readeat bookstores located in busy areas of Kyiv, are closing. The chain’s owner, Dmytro Feliksov, initially tried to sell the businesses, but there were no takers. What will happen to the book market next is difficult to predict. As with almost everything in Ukraine at the moment, much depends on Ukrainian air defense capabilities.
The general sense of uncertainty now extends to the previously impeccable passenger Railway service, Ukrzaliznytsia. Trains are repeatedly stopped en route. Recently, trains from Poland to Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia were delayed by up to 10 hours.
Even in this precarious situation, the Ukrainian government is managing to find cause for a modicum of cautious optimism. For example, there’s the recent agreement with Turkey for the purchase of hundreds of thousands of artillery shells and several hundred missiles.
President Zelensky has also announced that the United States still intends to supply Ukraine with some Patriot missiles each month. Indeed, any deliveries, no matter how small, will have a positive impact on the grim statistics of the war – the number of destroyed warehouses, factories, and residential buildings and, most importantly, on the number of lives lost.

articles.title: North Korea steps up hacking with AI and deepfakes
articles.body:
- North Korea-linked groups carried out 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea targeted 19 times, the most of any country.
- Combined attacks from North Korea, China and Russia totaled 158 incidents, up 7.5 percent from the prior six months, according to S2W.
North Korea-linked hacking groups launched 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea absorbing 19 of them, the most of any country, the Korea Times reported, citing a new threat intelligence report from cybersecurity firm S2W.
The figure makes North Korea the most active state-backed threat actor globally over the period, ahead of China’s 33 incidents and Russia’s 26. Combined attacks from all three countries totaled 158 between January and June, up 7.5 percent from 147 in the second half of last year. Most of that growth came in the first quarter, driven by intensified activity from North Korean and Russian groups.
North Korea’s attack volume rose 13.8 percent compared with the previous six months, according to the S2W report. The United States was the second most targeted country by North Korean actors, with eight recorded attacks.
Pyongyang-linked groups concentrated on the cryptocurrency, IT and software development sectors, using fake job postings, code repository infiltration, generative AI and deepfakes to gain access. South Korean cybersecurity firm AhnLab has separately tracked North Korean-linked spear phishing campaigns against South Korean targets this year using malicious LNK and CHM file attachments to deploy backdoors and infostealers.
Russian-linked attacks rose 30 percent to 26 incidents, with 10 aimed at Ukraine. Russian groups also expanded into Eastern Europe, striking Poland and Romania twice each, targeting European government and military organizations alongside their Ukraine-focused activity. The S2W report found Russian operations increasingly combined intelligence gathering with destructive attacks meant to disrupt or destroy systems.
China-linked attacks fell 17.5 percent, from 40 to 33 incidents, with Chinese groups sustaining long-term espionage operations against the telecommunications sector while expanding into Southeast Asia and the Middle East. S2W’s analysis found Chinese operators relied on legitimate cloud APIs, VPNs and network tunneling tools alongside malware to maintain extended access to compromised networks.
Across all three countries, S2W identified 15 unique exploited vulnerabilities used in 19 separate incidents during the first half. North Korean groups relied primarily on social engineering and tricking users into executing malicious files, while Chinese groups exploited vulnerabilities in public-facing servers and network edge devices. Russian groups favored document-based malware along with webmail and network device vulnerabilities. Phishing, exploitation of public server vulnerabilities and abuse of proxy and cloud services were common across all three.
The report projected that infiltration of software development ecosystems, long-term access to telecommunications and infrastructure networks, and destructive operations tied to geopolitical conflicts will continue into the second half of the year. S2W also flagged Iran-linked groups as a risk to South Korean manufacturing, aviation and energy companies through Middle East-based supply chain attacks, saying the threat warrants close monitoring.
A cybersecurity expert cited in the report said organizations need to move beyond fragmented defenses focused solely on email and malware blocking toward integrated security frameworks covering development environments, supply chains, internet-facing assets, cloud systems and AI environments. The expert also called for stronger intrusion detection, immediate rotation of account credentials, and the buildup of immutable backup and recovery systems.

articles.title: The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
The memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the war between Iran and the US expired on Monday, increasing the risk of a slide back towards open conflict and heightening uncertainty over a diplomatic settlement.
As the deadline edged closer, there was little sign of political will in either Washington or Tehran to extend the 60-day deal or return to the negotiating table.
Instead, the two sides have continued to trade threats, with US President Donald Trump threatening last week to declare the Strait of Hormuz an American territory and Iranian officials signalling readiness to return to war.
Here's what you need to know about the deal and why it failed.
What was agreed?
The interim deal was signed on 17 June by Trump and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and came following weeks of high-stakes diplomacy led by Pakistan and Qatar. It kick-started a two-month period during which the two sides committed to the ambitious goal of agreeing to a comprehensive peace agreement settling the intractable dispute over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Kicking the nuclear issue to future negotiations, the MoU was a stop-gap measure that nonetheless sought to address the most immediate crises by imposing a region-wide ceasefire and re-opening the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the deal, both sides agreed to immediately and permanently end military operations across all fronts, including in Lebanon, and to refrain from threats or the use of force.
To resolve the crisis in the strait, the US agreed to lift its blockade on Iranian ports within 30 days in return for Iran lifting restrictions on traffic and demining the area. Tehran said it would waive all fees for 60 days while the final deal was being negotiated. Crucially, it separated the strait's future status from the US-Iran negotiations, empowering Tehran to work with Oman to decide how it would be administered after the war.
Meanwhile, the US agreed to terminate all sanctions on Iran, issue waivers for its oil exports, and unlock some of its frozen assets. It also committed to develop a plan that would see at least $300 billion invested in Iran's reconstruction and economic development.
Iran reiterated its commitment not to seek nuclear weapons and agreed to freeze all nuclear activity while negotiations for a final deal continued.
Why has it failed?
Iran and the US showed goodwill in the days after the agreement, travelling to Switzerland on 21 June for what was the highest-level meeting between Iranian and American officials in decades. The following day, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Iran's oil exports for two months.
But things began to unravel in the subsequent weeks, with the countries trading accusations of breaching the accord.
On 26 June, Trump accused Iran of a "foolish violation" after a cargo ship was attacked in the Strait. Two days later, Tehran said Washington had broken the agreement following renewed US strikes. At the heart of the disagreement was the strait, which US officials continued to insist should be returned to its pre-war status quo. Iranian officials meanwhile bristled as Trump resumed his incendiary rhetoric, which they said violated the deal.
Officials from both countries soon declared the death of the MoU, and by the middle of July the ceasefire had all but collapsed. For two weeks, the US bombarded southern Iran while Tehran resumed heavy strikes across the Gulf.
Since a fragile peace was restored at the end of the month, there have been few signs that the warring countries are prepared to return to the negotiating table. Instead, both countries have returned to sabre-rattling and contesting control of the strait. Meanwhile, there has been no movement on US sanctions or Iran's frozen assets, while the American military has reimposed its blockade.
"The expiration of the MoU is, in one sense, the formal recognition of a reality that had already emerged," Neil Quilliam, Middle East foreign policy specialist at Chatham House, told The New Arab.
Both countries had already called the deal into question and accused one another of breaking its terms. "In that respect, the end of the MoU confirms the death of a framework that was already struggling to survive," he said.
What happens now?
The wider significance of its expiry lies in what happens next.
"If no alternative framework emerges, both sides will have greater freedom to pursue coercive measures, including military pressure, without the constraints, however weak, imposed by the agreement," Quilliam said. "This increases uncertainty and the risk of miscalculation."
Rather than threatening a military attack, Trump officials have instead signalled a return to economic pressure, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowing to impose measures that "have never been seen in the history of economic isolation".
The American military's ability to continue defending against Iranian attacks has been called into question in recent weeks following reports of a severe depletion of missile interceptors. It has also been said to have used "virtually all" of its precision long-range missiles.
Iran meanwhile has vowed to resume the war if the US does not agree to its demands. An Iranian official threatened on Monday to go "fully offensive" and escalate in the Gulf in a bid to break the US blockade.
Quilliam said the most likely outcome is a prolonged period of on-off confrontation. Neither side will likely risk a major regional war, but the profound lack of trust will continue to impede meaningful negotiations.
"Barring a major provocation, both Washington and Tehran appear more likely to manage tensions than seek a direct military showdown," he said.
"The danger is that prolonged instability creates repeated opportunities for miscalculation, making the conflict harder to contain over time."

articles.title: Russian strike cripples Ukraine’s largest steel plant
articles.body:
Russian strike cripples Ukraine’s largest steel plant
Ukraine’s largest steel plant has partially suspended production after a Russian missile strike damaged key facilities.
Located in Krivoy Rog, Dnepropetrovsk Region, ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog is an integrated steelworks that produces rolled products, including steel used in Ukrainian weapons and military equipment, according to the Russian military.
In a Telegram post on Sunday, the company said the overnight attack had damaged “the main energy and blast-furnace production facilities” and partially halted operations. It added that specialists were assessing the extent of the destruction and the prospects and timeframe for recovery.
The Russian Defense Ministry confirmed striking workshops at the metallurgical complex, saying the site was targeted in a combined attack involving ground- and air-launched precision weapons and long-range drones.
The overnight operation also targeted an oil refinery in Kremenchug, Poltava Region. In Kiev, Russian forces struck Fire Point, which produces components, warheads, and solid-fuel boosters for Flamingo cruise missiles.
Another target was Kiev-111, a facility operated by Ukrdefense Company that manufactures components for attack drones, Khrushch interceptor UAVs, and Harpia anti-aircraft drones.
Russia has intensified strikes on Ukrainian defense-related facilities and logistics following a 40-day “operation of influence” announced by Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in late June. Kiev portrayed the campaign of long-range drone attacks as an effort to force Moscow into negotiations on its terms.
Over the following weeks, Ukraine targeted Russian oil refineries, logistics warehouses operated by retailer Wildberries – often described as “Russia’s Amazon” – and sites far from the front line.
Moscow described the attacks on energy infrastructure, residential buildings, and logistics hubs as terrorism, saying they killed dozens of civilians.
As the deadline expired in early August without the campaign achieving its objectives, the head of Zelensky’s office, Kirill Budanov, dismissed the significance of the timeframe, claiming that “what matters is the result.”
The ensuing Russian strikes on Ukraine’s defense industry have depleted Kiev's stock of Patriot interceptor missiles, leaving air-defense crews “helpless” against the barrages, according to the Financial Times. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians.

articles.title: August 16 Strike on Kamensky Defense Plant Damaged Five Production Buildings and Air Defense Systems
articles.body:
The drone strike on the Kamensky Combine plant on the night of August 16 damaged five production facilities.
Exilenova+ published a satellite image with an analysis of the damage.
The air defense systems protecting the plant were also hit. These included positions of a Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft artillery system and multifunctional target illumination and guidance radars for S-300/S-400 systems, where signs of fire were observed.
Notably, the production buildings were additionally protected by earth berms and anti-drone nets. However, judging by the imagery, the nets failed to provide adequate protection: some buildings show roof penetrations and torn anti-drone nets.
According to Yuriy Slyusar, governor of the Rostov region, Russian air defense systems shot down more than 150 UAVs over the region that night. However, he did not disclose the total number of drones involved in the attack.
The FIRMS service detected a thermal signature following the attack at 1:14 a.m. on August 16. It persisted and expanded until 2:20 a.m.
According to the OSINT resource VARTA, FSE Kamensky Combine is one of the largest chemical enterprises in southern Russia and has the status of an anchor enterprise.
The plant is located at coordinates 48.29943029832428, 40.17984650497104, approximately 10-15 km from Ukraine’s state border.
Due to its proximity to Ukraine, the facility is within range of a significant number of weapons systems in service with the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
The company’s primary line of business is the production of military equipment. The plant manufactures artillery shells, propellants, explosives, detonators, fuzes, primers, precursors, and other ammunition components.
The facility’s grounds have already been targeted by Ukrainian airstrikes. On December 20, 2024, the Ukrainian Air Force attacked the facility with Storm Shadow cruise missiles.
At the time, analysts from the CyberBoroshno group published satellite imagery showing critical damage to two buildings at the plant’s production site.
