articles.title: US moves to ramp up naval anti-ballistic missile production
articles.body:
Boeing has signed seven-year framework agreements to increase production of key components for the Standard Missile-3, a ship-launched anti-ballistic missile designed to intercept threats outside the Earth’s atmosphere.
The United States is moving to increase production of Standard Missile-3 anti-ballistic missile interceptors, with Boeing signing new seven-year framework agreements covering critical hardware used in both the SM-3 Block IB and Block IIA variants, according to the company.
The agreements with the U.S. Department of War and Raytheon, an RTX business and prime contractor for the missile, are intended to increase Boeing’s output of avionics and ejector assemblies needed for higher production rates of complete SM-3 interceptors. Boeing said the three parties will begin ramping up production ahead of a final multi-year award while negotiations continue under the new framework.
The SM-3 is a ship-launched anti-ballistic missile used as part of the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system. Its principal role is to intercept ballistic missiles during the midcourse portion of their flight, when the target can be travelling outside the Earth’s atmosphere. Rather than relying on an explosive warhead, the interceptor uses a kinetic kill vehicle intended to destroy the target through the force of a direct collision.
That makes the SM-3 distinct from shorter-range air-defence weapons intended primarily to engage aircraft, cruise missiles or other threats within the atmosphere. The missile is designed for ballistic missile defence, providing US and allied forces with an exo-atmospheric interception capability from Aegis-equipped warships and related missile-defence infrastructure.
Bob Ciesla, vice president of Boeing Precision Engagement Systems, said, as quoted in a news update: “This gives us a clear demand signal to build and deliver SM-3 interceptors at the levels needed to counter threats.” He added: “The SM-3 is an essential part of the layered air and missile defense architecture that protects the U.S. and its allies worldwide.”
Both the Block IB and Block IIA variants are covered by the new arrangement. The Block IIA is the larger and more capable development of the weapon, designed to provide greater range and engagement capability against ballistic missile threats. Boeing’s role includes producing avionics and ejector assemblies, components that must be available in sufficient numbers if Raytheon is to increase output of complete missiles.
The decision to begin increasing production before completion of the multi-year contract is intended to give industry a clearer demand signal and reduce the delay between a procurement decision and higher delivery rates. Boeing said the framework supports the administration’s effort to strengthen what it calls the “Arsenal of Freedom” and aligns with Pentagon acquisition reforms intended to accelerate the delivery of priority weapons.
The SM-3 agreement also follows an existing arrangement involving Boeing, the Department of War and Lockheed Martin to increase production of seekers for the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptor.

articles.title: ‘The most terrifying 11 hours of my life’: What really happens when you cross Russia’s border? Meduza’s readers share their stories.
articles.body:
‘The most terrifying 11 hours of my life’: What really happens when you cross Russia’s border? Meduza’s readers share their stories.
Crossing Russia’s border has become an increasingly fraught experience in recent years, whether you’re returning home or leaving the country. Last week, Meduza asked Russian readers to share their experiences crossing the border. While we expected to hear mostly from Russians living abroad, we also received dozens of accounts from people who still live in Russia and travel overseas. Not every crossing involved questioning or delays — some readers told us they passed through without incident. Here’s what they had to say.
Anton
I live in Russia but travel abroad for vacations. Border guards have questioned me twice in the past two years — the system flags me for additional screening, and both times were unpleasant. I live in Russia 11 months out of every 12, so it’s incredibly disappointing that this keeps happening. Why can I travel to any country in the world and get let in without a problem, but get interrogated when I come home?
Dmitry
In the four years since I left, I’ve been to Russia three times, to set up my business and visit my parents. Crossing the border went smoothly all three times, without incident or extra interrogation. They always ask on what grounds I live in Europe, and I show my residence permit. Surprisingly — and unfortunately — I have nothing unpleasant to report, except that every time, I feel like a tourist in my own country.
Anatoly
I travel once a year, for a couple of months. Every time I arrive, they ask the same questions: why, where to, where from, what do you do. My tip: bring your internal passport. They always ask for it, and things go faster if you have it. Nothing ever happened at departure — until the last time I left.
In August, they didn’t stop at [questioning me] at the booth — [the border guard] took me to a room and interrogated me for half an hour: who I am, what I do, where I live, with whom, where my relatives are, hand over your phone (I gave him a clean one), who I talk to, do I have anyone in Ukraine? I decided I would not go back to Russia again.
Zhenechka
My last entry was in the fall of 2024, when I waited 11 hours to be screened. I was lucky my laptop stayed with my wife, who had time to wipe it clean while I called her from other people’s phones. Those were the most terrifying 11 hours of my life — primal fear brings on all kinds of thoughts, and I had chat histories and payment records [that could get someone prosecuted].
Arkady
I traveled [to Russia] once, in December 2025 — the only [time] since I moved to Israel in 2022. I came for New Year’s, to visit friends, walk around familiar places, and pick up some belongings.
I prepared thoroughly for the trip. I have no history of detentions or prosecution in Russia, but I do have plenty of posts, photos, and donation records (to Meduza, for example!) that I wouldn’t want Russian authorities to see. I’m also transgender and have a nervous system disorder, which creates extra problems at any checkpoint — tremors and nervous reactions mean I get searched for drugs more often. In Israel, it took a 20-minute body scan for officers to find the organs needed for my passport, which was pretty funny, but fairly safe.
For the trip, I took my brother’s old phone and installed Russian apps I used to use — Yandex Mail, Russian Railways, 2GIS, and so on. I loaded some music for the trip, downloaded wallpaper pictures and plane tickets, made sure I had no Ukrainian contacts, searched for random things on Google, and poked around on YouTube to build up a search history — just to have one — and went.
The plane landed at Domodedovo at seven in the morning, and I spent the next five hours at the airport going through checks of every kind. At passport control, they asked a lot of strange questions: what were you doing in Poland? Is this your passport? You’ve changed so much — my Russian and Israeli passports have photos from before and after HRT — but the personal data matched, since I’d managed to change it before the repressive laws took effect, which made things easier.
After passport control, they took me to a security checkpoint, where I sat for four hours in a fenced-off pen of chairs. Officers called people by last name from there into an office for questioning and a phone search. My conversation with the border guard went something like this:
“Where are all your messaging apps? How do you communicate, by phone calls?”
“Yeah.”
“Where’s your social media?”
“I don’t use it.”
“You’re sure you don’t have a second phone?”
“I’m sure.”
“And if I find one?”
“You won’t.”
Then another officer came in and said, “Just take it to Igor, let him run it through his [some abbreviation, I don’t remember], it’ll take five minutes.” They carried my phone off to another office to “run it through” some kind of plug-in device.
I sat in the pen without my phone or passports, talking with the people around me — most of those waiting for screening had some connection to Ukraine or lacked Russian citizenship. I remember a mother and her adult daughter who had left Crimea in 2010; the mother carried Ukrainian and Israeli documents, while the daughter had only Israeli ones. “They ask why we don’t have Russian passports since we’re from Crimea. But we left before Crimea became Russian, and try explaining that to them now.”
Some people there travel on business every year and go through these checks every single time. […] After four hours of waiting, they returned my phone and passports and told me I could go. Next came a baggage search that took another hour — they emptied my backpack and suitcase completely, filmed the process on a department camera, and inspected every single item. […] After that, I was finally let out of the airport.
Anatoly
For family reasons, I’ve visited Russia six times since November 2025. Each time, I expected some kind of problem at the border, but nothing serious ever happened.
The real problem is the car line to enter Russia — the fastest crossing took about four hours, the longest about 17.
They checked my phone only once, and since I don’t bring my work phone, no additional questions came up. Maybe I’ve just been lucky, but I’ve had no problems with border guards over all these trips. Given that the country is at war, checks like this strike me as understandable, even a necessary security measure. But things could have been much worse.
Ksenia
I fly once a year to visit family, and it usually goes smoothly. But in October 2025, I was pulled in for questioning that lasted four hours. They went through all my things, checked my phone, and took my fingerprints. The interrogation covered who I talk to, who my relatives are, whether I know anyone in Ukraine, and so on. They asked about social media but didn’t check it. It worked out — but I won’t be going again.
Oleg
I come to Russia twice a year to visit relatives — and to buy medicine, tea, and so on. I usually have to answer unpleasant questions: where did you come from, what were you doing there, with whom, what’s your job, where do you permanently live.
The last time, in July, I landed at a regional airport and wasn’t let through because officers didn’t like my answer of “tourism” after a six-month absence from Russia. After waiting 10–15 minutes, I was called into an office for a talk. A different officer let me explain everything fairly quickly, and they didn’t try to look at my phone. It’s also annoying that customs officers X-ray luggage on arrival, and in some places there’s a full customs search on departure as well.
Anna
I mostly live in Russia, but I go to Italy for a month every year to see relatives there. There are other trips sometimes too, but the experience is roughly the same overall. I get through passport control fine, but I’ve noticed more questions lately — and I’ve heard from others that questioning has increased in general, especially for men (purpose of the trip, return tickets, and so on).
The last time — and this wasn’t even at the border, just going through the green channel exit at Pulkovo — they asked a lot of questions: purpose of the trip, how many days I’d flown for, where I’d originally flown in from. Fine. But then they suddenly asked how many euros I’d entered the country with and how much I had left, including how much I’d spent on purchases. I said “definitely under 500 euros in purchases,” and then they asked how much I’d entered with — the difference came out to around 250–300 euros. The young border guard said, “the math doesn’t quite add up, but fine,” and let me through.
I guess I’ll need to keep my receipts so the math works out next time. Before this, there were no questions of this kind, and in general I was rarely questioned at all.
Andrey
I come to Russia once a year to see my parents, and every time I depart from Moscow, the electronic passport control system flags me for additional screening by a border service officer. That’s when the real ordeal begins. Already in line, it’s clear many other passengers are in the same situation — they’re leaving Russia on one-way tickets.
The border guard’s own behavior adds to the tension: he scans the passport on several computers, cross-checks the data against every available database, keeps swiveling in his chair, and every so often stares intently at me, as if gauging my reaction. The atmosphere is so tense that you can’t help feeling he’s hunting for the smallest detail that might look suspicious.
Compared with passport control in other countries, the wariness and suspicion toward passengers here feels especially acute.
Anton
I travel once or twice a year to see my family, always arriving and departing through Moscow.
Fortunately, I’ve never had any problems — no questions, ever.
Alexander
I live in Russia and travel abroad a couple of times a year. I was tried for discrediting the military in 2023 and fined 40,000 rubles. In the fall of 2025, I flew to Paris and passed through passport control with no problems.
In August 2026, I decided to fly from Mineralnye Vody to Armenia for three days, just to walk around. Going through passport control there, a female officer told me to wait for additional screening and kept my passport. I was called into an office, where two officers asked me to unlock my phone and hand it over, which I did. One scrolled through it while the other asked questions: why are you flying, what’s your job, who are your parents, which countries have you visited since 2014, have you ever been convicted, do you have access to state secrets?
Inside, I was panicking that they were scrolling through my phone — personal messages, browser history — but I didn’t let it show. They wrote down my phone’s IMEI number and asked me to sign a paper agreeing to take a polygraph test whenever summoned. They said that if I didn’t sign, I’d stay there another three hours and miss my flight, so I signed. Then they told me to wait outside but kept my phone. As I understand it, they copied all the data off it to study later — or maybe installed something of their own on it too. Who knows.
On the way back to Russia three days later, there was no interrogation, but they again took my unlocked phone and carried it off to an office for about 40 minutes.
Khaidar
After I moved to Germany, I wanted to keep visiting my parents. In Russia, they usually just asked where I’d come from and where I was going. [Then they would say]: have a good trip!
In April 2025, they took my passport and examined it: Why Foreign Ministry of Russia? I live and work in Berlin! They took the passport and [said]: wait. The whole busload of us waited eight hours! Then came the interrogation: How did you get your passport? What’s your attitude toward the war in Ukraine? Toward Putin? Toward [the] Crocus [City Hall terrorist attack] (I’m Muslim)? Do you pray? And a phone check.
Ivan
I’ve lived in Germany for seven years now but go to Russia about once a year to see my parents. I’d never had problems at the border, so I didn’t prepare much — I didn’t wipe my phone or delete any messages, figuring I had nothing to hide. This time, after passport control, they asked me to wait. An officer came over and asked if I had a second phone. I said no.
“What about old phones?”
I said there was an old iPhone with a cracked screen lying at home.
He asked:
“Where exactly at home?”
At first I thought it was just a routine question, so I said it was in a desk drawer. They took me to a separate room and asked me to unlock my current phone. The officer scrolled through the photos for quite a while. There was nothing special there: trips, food, friends, screenshots. Then he stopped on a photo of me standing next to trash bins in Berlin.
“Why did you take a photo with trash bins?”
I explained that a friend had just happened to photograph me on the way home.
“Just happened?”
He asked me to open the photo’s date. Then the geolocation. Then he zoomed in on one of the bins. There was a sticker on it that said, “No to war.”
I hadn’t even noticed that sticker before. The officer asked:
“Do you agree with what it says?”
I said I sort my trash. He asked again:
“What do you mean?”
I had to explain the German waste-sorting system. After that, the conversation somehow shifted to plastic for a long while. He asked why bottle caps are now attached to the bottles and whether that annoys me. I said it sometimes does. He wrote something down. Then they found a photo of breakfast. There was bread, cheese, coffee, and a jar of jam.
“What kind of jam?”
I said French.
“Why French?”
I said it was on sale. He asked me to open my banking app and find the jam purchase. We couldn’t find the purchase, because my girlfriend had bought the jam. Then the officer asked for my girlfriend’s last name. I told him.
“Is she a German citizen?”
“Yes.”
“Why does she buy you French jam?”
I no longer knew what the right answer was, so I said:
“Because we live together.”
After this he first looked at me very closely.
“So you have a shared household?”
I said, probably, yes. He wrote something down again. Next they opened Telegram. Among the recent messages was a conversation with my mom. Mom had written: “Everything’s ready for your arrival.” The officer asked:
“Ready for what, exactly?”
I said the room.
“What room?”
“My old room.”
“Why is it still yours if you’ve lived in Germany for seven years?”
I said that’s just what my parents call it. He asked me to call my mom.
Mom picked up and immediately asked:
“Did you get through?”
The officer raised his eyebrows.
“Get through what?”
Mom explained she meant the border. Then, for some reason, she added:
“We’ve already put the potatoes on.”
The officer asked:
“Why did you put potatoes on?”
Mom said:
“To boil.”
After that, he asked to put the call on speaker and spent about 10 minutes talking with my mom about how many potatoes she’d bought, exactly where, and why she’d decided to boil them before I even arrived.
At one point, mom asked:
“Young man, would you like some potatoes?”
Pavel
[I go to Russia] once every six months to a year. There have never been problems on entry — border guards usually let me through quickly and rarely ask questions, maybe because my arriving flights are from Yerevan or Istanbul. There are usually more questions on departure, about the purpose of the trip and how long it’s for, but even those feel like they’re asked out of boredom.
The only unpleasant experience was in 2022, when they made me turn out all my pockets and flipped through all my books and notebooks looking for cash. Otherwise, everything always goes smoothly. The most interesting moment: border guards once asked to see my foreign diploma, just out of curiosity.
Yekaterina
I come once a year to visit my mom and see friends. This summer I traveled alone with two children (ages 3 and 7) through the Estonian border, at the Koidula crossing. To get there, we took a ferry from Helsinki to Tallinn and spent the night there. In the morning we took a commuter train and rode four hours to Koidula. This used to be probably the most deserted border crossing, located somewhere in the middle of nowhere.
But at the start of summer, hours were cut at the other Estonian crossing point, Narva (where people almost always stand in line for a whole day or longer), and apparently some people decided to look for other routes. So by the time we got to the border, there was already a line, though it seemed small — you have to walk about a kilometer from the train station along the road and then through the bushes, and everyone tries to hurry there right away, so it turns into this sad race of people with suitcases and rolling bags.
The line moved gradually, and the Estonian border guards and customs officers at Koidula are pretty nice, friendly people. But then a double-decker bus arrived, and all its passengers — about 50 people, probably — were let ahead of the line. Still, credit to the Estonians: everyone got through in about an hour, probably. We got through without any problems too, and started moving toward the Russian checkpoint.
And then, around a bend, we saw a strange crowd of people gathered in front of a closed gate. It turned out the Russian border guards didn’t want people crowding up there, because of that bus we’d seen, plus an earlier one, and they were checking them for an extremely long time. So people were standing in front of this ridiculous gate in the heat, waiting. An hour, two hours — some had already been waiting four hours.
It was simply unbearable. Elderly people, families with children in the heat. And about 50 meters (about 164 feet) away was the Russian checkpoint, this nice big building with trees and shade… But no, you wait here. People were outraged, people talked to “the person in charge,” but they weren’t authorized to split up the crowd. It was very hard and upsetting.
Anonymous
I flew from Serbia to Nizhny Novgorod to see my parents, glad they’d introduced direct flights. Next time I’ll fly through Moscow, screw it. They pulled aside almost half the people for questioning. They asked whose Crimea it was, whether I supported the SVO, why I’d left the country, and asked to see my Instagram, Facebook, Telegram. They asked me to explain visible tattoos.
Everything on my phone was clean, and I showed all of it — I had the feeling that if I refused, it would only get worse, but still, the fact of it. They searched my contacts for numbers starting with +380. Then they said “welcome home” with this little smirk. It felt like they just enjoy terrorizing people. I read afterward that this happens a lot in Nizhny Novgorod. The woman behind me in line had children with her.
Klim
Since the war began, I’ve been to Russia four times by plane and twice by car. There was a two-and-a-half-hour interrogation in Zhukovsky about my attitude toward the SVO, an examination of my phone contacts and reading of my Telegram messages, and then they took my phone away entirely for “technical analysis.”
Ivan
I should start by saying that I’m a citizen of Kyrgyzstan, one of the Central Asian republics with especially close political, economic, and cultural ties to Russia. Russian has official status there, Russian media occupies a prominent place, and the republic pursues a fairly accommodating policy toward Russia. Kyrgyzstan has even repeatedly found itself at risk of secondary sanctions because of its trade and economic ties with Russia.
We have relatives living in Russia, so from time to time we visit and stay with them in the Kaliningrad region. I’ve been to Russia in 2021, 2023, and 2025. During the first two trips, nothing came up at the border at all — everything went completely routinely: I said hello, handed over my passport, got a stamp, and moved on to my next flight. But 2025 turned out differently. That was when I first felt, through my own experience, what I had previously only known as other people’s stories about bias against migrants and people from Central Asia.
My mother and I arrived at Sheremetyevo together. At passport control we ended up in different lines. Mine was moving more slowly, hers faster, so at some point I moved closer to her and ended up at the neighboring window. Her turn came. She handed over her passport, the border guard stamped it, and let her through. I submitted my passport right after. My mother stepped a bit further away and waited for me by the exit. The border guard took my passport and said dryly, almost angrily: “Go wait. You’ll be called.” That was it — no explanation of where to go, what to wait for, how long it would take, or why I was even being held. We had no phone connection; connecting to Wi-Fi at Sheremetyevo without verification through a Russian phone number was impossible at the time.
When my mother realized I wasn’t being let through, she asked the border guard not to send her on ahead and to let her stay next to me. He replied irritably: “No. You go ahead, he stays.” The door closed. We ended up on opposite sides of it: without contact, without explanations, in complete uncertainty. What felt especially humiliating was not understanding what I was even guilty of. I hadn’t broken any rules — I had registered in advance with ruID and come to the country on an ordinary private visit, to see relatives. So why was I being treated as if I were some kind of suspect?
Meanwhile, right in front of me, citizens of Russia and Belarus were let through without any trouble, while many people with Central Asian passports and features typical of the region were sent to wait. The border guard’s window was free for a while, so I decided to go up again and ask what I should do, who exactly was supposed to call me, and for what reason. “I already told you: you’ll be called!” he barked. I had to step back. I stood near the passage and waited. After a while, through the general noise, I heard an announcement over the loudspeaker: someone was being called by name to go to a room with a specific number. That’s how I first learned there were special rooms nearby for additional screening.
I went looking for them. People had already gathered near these rooms, most of them from Central Asia. And at that moment it felt especially strange to think about all the talk of customs unions, economic integration, friendship between peoples, and “allied relations.” At the level of official rhetoric, we’re partners and friends. But standing there, I didn’t feel any of that at all. The situation was made worse because we had a connecting flight from Sheremetyevo to Kaliningrad three hours after landing. By that point, only about an hour and 40 minutes remained before departure, and there was still no clarity.
People were called into the rooms one by one. From those waiting, I heard that officers there ask detailed questions about the purpose of the trip, demand that phones be unlocked, and go through their contents. I was never called into one of those rooms myself. But I remember very clearly the feeling of total helplessness — when your passport is somewhere with someone you don’t know, no one explains anything, you can’t reach a loved one, and you don’t even know if you’ll make your next flight.
Time passed. Finally a border service officer came out with a whole stack of passports and started reading off names. After that, they took us back to passport control. About 40 people stood waiting for their names to be called, then went up to the window one at a time. When I was finally let go, about half an hour remained before the flight to Kaliningrad. I ran out into the terminal with two heavy bags. My mother was waiting there, in tears. That moment, I think, stuck with me more than anything else — not the screening itself, not the lost time, not even the fear of missing the flight, but how easily a person can be left in complete uncertainty, separated from a loved one, without anyone bothering to say even a few human words to them.
At that moment I felt a lot of anger. I wanted Russian citizens to one day be met with the same “hospitality” in our country: to have their passports taken without explanation, to have border officers bark at them the same way, to be separated from relatives, sent to wait for who knows what, have their phones checked, and be made to feel like criminals before they’d even done anything.
But setting emotions aside, the problem runs deeper than a simple wish to respond in kind. I understand there’s serious tension in Russia around migration — problems with crime, illegal migration, the integration of newcomers, the work of law enforcement, and flaws in the migration system itself. All of this can and should be debated. But responsibility for state migration policy lies, first and foremost, with the state. And if a system is built over years that simultaneously draws in millions of foreign workers, poorly controls migration flows, allows abuses, and then tries to make up for its own failures with suspicion toward everyone with the “wrong” passport or appearance — that is not a solution to the problem.
An ordinary person legally crossing the border shouldn’t automatically become a suspect just because they were born in Dushanbe, Bishkek, Tashkent, or any other city in Central Asia. A state’s border has every right to be strict. But strictness and humiliation are not the same thing, just as screening and contempt are not the same thing. And security doesn’t require giving up basic human decency.
Anonymous
Over the past two years, I’ve traveled to Russia for family reasons about once every six months. In my case, the red flag for Russian border guards is that I renounced my Russian citizenship. At passport control, I’m always asked about it, both on entry and on exit.
The most unpleasant case was when I was sent for a conversation with an officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. The conversation lasted about 15–20 minutes. They asked me about my reasons for renouncing citizenship, my job, connections to government agencies in my new country of citizenship, whether I’d traveled to Ukraine, and my attitude toward the war.
They tried to look at my phone, but I’d brought a clean one. When the FSB officer realized that, he immediately lost interest in it — though I still had to explain why my phone was clean. Toward the end of the conversation, they even asked how I had a child if I’d never been married…
My advice to people who have renounced Russian citizenship and travel to Russia: always carry a copy of the certificate confirming you renounced citizenship. They may ask for it at passport control.
Dmitry
I travel every six months, mostly crossing the border by car from Belarus through Lithuania into Kaliningrad; I have dual citizenship with visa-free access to the Schengen area. The Belarusians have always conducted fairly perfunctory interviews on entry into Belarus, and on exit there are usually no questions and only a basic search, or none at all.
But in July, entering the Kaliningrad region from the Lithuanian side at Chernyakhovsk, I went through an extremely unpleasant screening — effectively an interrogation with fingerprinting and biometric sample collection and a four-hour interview, during which FSB border service officers read through all my messenger correspondence, went through all my contacts and photos, compiled my entire life story, and took very detailed notes on four typed pages. They probed my political views, asked whether I belonged to any banned movements, in particular the LGBTQ+ movement, asked about my job, and took my boss’s contact information.
I left demoralized and humiliated, fully aware that I would never cross a Russian checkpoint by car again. After that, the 12–19-hour wait at Belarusian customs, with surprisingly friendly staff, doesn’t seem so bad.
P. S. My phone wasn’t always in my line of sight — officers stepped out with it several times — so I can’t guarantee that no third-party software was installed on it.
Nailya
I flew to Russia for two weeks in the second half of May. It was time to renew my internal passport. I’d last been there in December 2021, so this was my first trip since the [full-scale] war began. Before that I used to fly twice a year, even during the pandemic, and nothing abnormal ever happened — it was always calm. This time, too, nothing happened to me.
I flew out of Kazan at the end of May. The room with the border guard booths is very small. There were something like four or five booths, I remember four lines, and people were packed tightly together because there wasn’t much space, the border guards worked slowly, and crowds built up.
Apparently, one line was specifically set aside for “non-Russians.” There was one family, Tajik I think, with a child, age 3 or 4, standing there for about 15 minutes. The man answered questions in fairly good Russian — the room is small, you can hear everything — but then they picked the child up, and the border guard started asking the child something, and the little girl couldn’t answer.
Then the border guard just started stupidly yelling across the whole hall: “Where did you get this certificate? You bought it, didn’t you? She doesn’t even speak Russian. Admit it — did you buy the certificate? How much did you pay, where did you buy it?”
He kept shouting like that for another five minutes, accusing and insulting this family, who were simply frozen with fear, in front of everyone. And no one came over to him, no one told him to stop; all his colleagues and superiors just kept working as if nothing were happening. It became unbearably disgusting and repulsive, both toward my fellow citizens and toward the country as a whole, where civil servants allow themselves to “talk” to people like that. Shameful.
Andrey
I was traveling from Russia to Kazakhstan in June 2025 when I was pulled off the train for additional screening. They demanded I unlock my smartphone — I refused. They held me at the station for almost a full day, beat me, and tortured me. I ended up having to give them access to all my devices. An X-ray eventually showed two broken ribs.
Nastya
I try to go to Russia every year. I love my hometown and my family and loved ones, and it’s very hard for me when I don’t see them for a long time. It’s always a little nerve-wracking, because since the war began I’ve openly spoken out against it on social media. My friends and relatives know my position. So do random people online.
Every time, I prepare my gadgets, wiping chat histories and browser history. I’ve never been checked. But sometimes there are unpleasant questions — unpleasant mainly because of the tone the border guards use. For some reason, women seem especially prone to this. Very hostile looks, as if you’re guilty simply for coming home to visit.
I really want to keep being able to come to Russia, and I’ll keep doing it for as long as I can.
Besides the rudeness and hostile looks from border guards, it’s unsettling when someone from the line gets taken off to a separate office. I’ve seen that happen a couple of times over my five trips.
Sonya
I hadn’t been back since 2022. In 202-something, I flew into my hometown with my young son. We got off the plane and were first in line for passport control. After the standard questions about my residence and permanent residence permits, the female border guard sent me to “sit off to the side.” After that, they questioned me at length about whether I’d had plastic surgery, whether I had a twin sister. They took me into a separate room and, shining a flashlight in my face and enlarging my passport photo, compared every millimeter.
Then they asked whether my son spoke Russian, went up to him, and asked who he was flying with. He was nervous and stayed quiet. They asked him my name, and he used the pet name he calls me at home. After that, yet another — the fourth — customs officer tried to scrutinize me, whispering to a colleague that “there used to be a mole on her cheek, and now there isn’t,” implying the passport wasn’t mine. They suggested I log into Gosuslugi to verify my identity. I refused, offering instead to show my internal passport. Finally, after about an hour and a half, they let us through.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Russia deploys 10 new bases near borders to launch jet drones against Ukraine – The Telegraph
articles.body:
Russia deploys 10 new bases near borders to launch jet drones against Ukraine – The Telegraph
Russia has built and expanded at least 10 military bases along its borders with Ukraine and Belarus, designed to launch large numbers of new jet-powered drones in an effort to systematically exhaust and break through Ukrainian air defences.
Source: an investigation by The Telegraph, based on analysis of satellite imagery, leaked documents and data from the DroneSec intelligence company
Details: Journalists and military analysts identified 59 mechanical launch rails along the Ukrainian and Belarusian borders. These rail catapults replace runways and allow heavy fixed-wing drones to be launched rapidly from locations close to the line of contact.
At least 20 of these launch rails have an extended design. Experts say they are intended to launch new high-speed jet-powered variants of long-range drones.
Some of the hubs were created by converting existing military bases and civilian airports, while other sites were built from scratch in rural areas.
Experts estimate that the scale of the expansion of storage infrastructure indicates that Moscow is preparing for a prolonged and more intensive air campaign. At one of the bases alone, storage facilities capable of holding more than 1,000 attack drones simultaneously have been identified. Construction of additional launch positions is still underway at a number of sites.
Drones are delivered directly to the launch sites from Russian military factories, including the production cluster in the Alabuga special economic zone in the Republic of Tatarstan.
According to leaked documents, new variants known as the Geran-4 and Geran-5 are equipped with jet engines, can carry an enhanced 90-kilogramme warhead and travel at significantly higher speeds, reducing the effectiveness of Ukrainian mobile fire groups.
In addition, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has warned that Russia is equipping Geran drones with air-to-air missiles to target Ukrainian aircraft involved in intercepting aerial assets over major cities.
The Kremlin has "significantly expanded" its drone network to "attack Ukraine and to hold Nato states at risk of such attacks", according to DroneSec CEO and founder Mike Monnik, who analysed satellite imagery.
Quote from Monnik: "This launch site expansion shows how Russia has expanded its ability to launch greater numbers of drones while at the same time using technology to make the types of drones used more difficult to intercept.
These two elements combine to enable a growing number of total unmanned aircraft systems Russia can use to attack Ukraine and increase the difficulty facing Ukrainian forces in intercepting newer Russian drone designs."
Details: Analysts warn that Russia's new jet-powered drones could also be used against European countries, with the location of some of the bases allowing Russian drones to reach Warsaw.

articles.title: Iraq's parliament probes US-Saudi strikes on PMF HQ
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq's parliament investigates US-Saudi strikes on PMF headquarters
Iraqi sources said the circumstances surrounding the US-Saudi strikes on the headquarters of Iraqi factions, which took place at the end of last month, remain unclear after statements circulated claiming that senior Iraqi leaders had advanced information of the strikes.
This prompted the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee to seek an investigation into the circumstances and host senior leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and prominent security officials to establish the facts and determine the details.
This strikes have set of growing repercussions, as well as doubts and questions raised in recent days about the security precautionary measures taken before the PMF headquarters were targeted and whether there had been any particular failure.
The committee, headed by MP Khalid al-Obeidi, issued an official letter inviting senior security and military officials, including PMF chief Falih al-Fayyadh and Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
Those invited also include the director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Abdul Amir al-Shammari; the army chief of staff, Abdul Amir Yarallah; and the senior Interior Ministry undersecretary, Hussein al-Awadi.
The letter stated that they would appear today at the committee's headquarters in the parliament building to determine why precautionary and security measures were not taken and why the headquarters was evacuated before the attack.
According to a member of the parliamentary committee, "The request to establish the facts and the attendance of the requested leaders came following accusations and statements that there had been advance information before the attack and that there had been a failure to perform the duty and evacuate the faction headquarters."
The member told The New Arab, on condition of anonymity, that "the committee is primarily focused on determining whether advance information about the strikes had reached the relevant agencies, which parties possessed it, and why urgent and decisive measures were not taken to address the situation before the airstrikes took place."
"The committee is carefully following the sequence of available intelligence information and the security measures that preceded the strikes to determine responsibilities and establish whether there were specific security gaps in the exchange of information and its intelligence verification and identify the parties or individuals responsible for this failure," the member added.
"Hosting the leaders and security officials will provide the committee with an opportunity to compare their statements with the information available to them," the source said, further stressing that "the hearings are part of an investigation that is not limited to determining the circumstances of the strike but also traces the information and establishes whether precautionary measures could have been taken in advance that might have prevented the casualties or reduced them."
The Iraqi government has repeatedly denied having prior knowledge of the strikes, but MPs and politicians have accused PMF leaders of possessing advance information about the targeting and failing to take sufficient precautions.
This has pushed the issue into a sensitive political arena that goes beyond the immediate security aspect.
Meanwhile, the PMF, which include the factions targeted in the strikes, rejected accusations against its chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, and claims that he had prior information about attacks on the headquarters and failed to inform the military units.
It described the accusations as "baseless claims that are not supported by any evidence or fact".
In a previous statement, the force said that "since the events in the region began months ago and until today, all its forces have been placed on alert, and two days before the strikes, all units were informed of the need to exercise the utmost caution and vigilance, which contributed to saving many lives and reducing the scale of the losses".
It said that "the fourth regiment of the 30th Brigade of the Popular Mobilisation did not take all the required preventive measures, resulting in the deaths of the largest number of its personnel during the attacks."
A sensitive issue
For his part, Iraqi political affairs specialist and academic Basim al-Azzawi said the issue was highly sensitive and that conflicting statements between accusations and denials involved political considerations.
He told TNA that "some parties may seek to use the issue of the strikes to achieve political gains, particularly given the sensitivity of the issue and its implications."
"The importance of the investigation lies in its ability to distinguish between security information and political responsibility and determine whether the failure, if established, resulted from weaknesses in the warning and information-sharing system, individual negligence by certain figures, or a broader failure in the management of the security issue," he added.
Iraqi official: PMF are part of armed forces
On Saturday, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said that "the PMF are part of the armed forces and that the decision to restrict weapons to the state targets entities operating outside the framework of the security institutions."
Maan made the remarks to the official Iraqi News Agency, INA.
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and their personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," he said.
He explained that "the entities covered by the restriction of weapons are those operating outside the framework of the state's security institutions".
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and under Law No. 40 of 2016, all its personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," Maan added.
He said that "the decision to restrict weapons to the state is intended to affirm that there is no parallel leadership or other leadership using weapons outside the framework of the state".
Sources inside the PMF in Iraq said on Wednesday, 12 August, that major changes are expected within the force, including the replacement of its current chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, who has been at this post since being formally appointed in 2020.
The changes also include the replacement of PMF Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
He emerged publicly and assumed his post after his predecessor, Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was assassinated by a US airstrike in January 2020.
The sources added to TNA that the changes are the first steps towards further integrating the PMF into Iraq's regular security and military system amid US pressure to restrict the weapons of Iran-aligned factions that are incorporated into and funded by the PMF itself.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Vote with your ruble: The Russian stock market is rejecting Putin’s official optimism
articles.body:
Russian stock indexes have plunged 30% over the past three months, approaching their lowest level since the start of the war. Under conditions of higher taxes, arbitrary property confiscations, falling investment, increasing war damage, and high interest rates, the value of Russian companies will continue to decline.
A company’s share price is determined by the market's estimates of its future profits, and market valuations can be systematically distorted. Nevertheless, they are the most reliable estimates available given the fact that buyers and sellers of assets have the strongest incentive to value them accurately. That is why a stock market index is an important indicator of the state of the economy: it reflects the profitability of major companies.
A country’s economic history can be written by tracking the performance of its stock market indexes. Their decline often foreshadows a contraction in GDP and other shocks in the real economy.
Russia’s main ruble-denominated stock market index — the Moscow Exchange Index (formerly the MICEX) — was first calculated in 1997. Before that, in 1995, the dollar-denominated RTS Index was introduced. Both started at 100 points. Over its entire history, the ruble-denominated Moscow Exchange Index has risen 22.2-fold, while the dollar-denominated RTS Index has risen only 8.8-fold — the difference being most readily attributable to the ruble's depreciation relative to the dollar over the past three decades (from the beginning of 1998 to the present day, the price of gold has risen 14.4-fold in dollar terms but 207-fold in rubles).
Incidentally, if an investor in Russian stocks had reinvested all the dividends received since 1998, the dollar value of the portfolio would have increased only 5.3-fold, while its ruble value would have risen 95-fold. Investing in gold would have produced much higher returns in either case.
War and Punishment
In the period August–December 2014, the dollar-denominated RTS Index suffered a sharp decline, while the ruble-denominated Moscow Exchange Index did not. The reason was simple: in 2014, following the imposition of Western sanctions, the Russian economy experienced not so much a stock market crisis as a ruble devaluation (and strictly speaking, this trend was a continuation of the major market collapse that had begun back in April 2011).
In the fall of 2021, the Russian stock market essentially anticipated the coming full-scale invasion of Ukraine and its dire consequences for both countries. From September through mid-November, the Moscow Exchange Index fluctuated mostly between 4,000 and 4,200 points — close to its historic high. However, when leading Western media outlets began reporting on the unprecedented buildup of Russian troops along the border with Ukraine starting in November, the trend turned negative. On November 10, then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken openly warned that possible Russian aggression against Ukraine would be a major mistake, and on November 19, The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence was taking the threat of a Russian invasion of Ukraine extremely seriously. “The United States does not believe this is a bluff,” the newspaper wrote of the Kremlin’s military preparations (this at a time when many observers, including the author of this article, could not believe that a major war was actually approaching).
The Russian stock market, however, assessed the situation accurately. It was on that very day, November 19, 2021, that the Moscow Exchange Index last held above the 4,000-point mark. By New Year’s, it had fallen to 3,800, and on the last trading day before the invasion, it closed at 3,085 points. The Moscow Exchange Index fell by a total of 28% in the four months preceding February 24, 2022, and fell another 33%, to 2,058 points, on that fateful day.
The RTS Index, which is denominated in U.S. dollars rather than rubles, followed a similar trajectory. Overall, the shock connected with the Russian invasion of Ukraine was comparable to the most severe economic crises in Russia's modern history (1998 and 2008).
The current downturn is less severe than those three — comparable instead to the pandemic-related decline of 2020 and the “Kursk” contraction of 2024. But in any case, from March through July 2026 there was not even a minor short-term correction back upwards: the Moscow Exchange Index fell for 19 consecutive weeks, an unprecedented streak, before a correction began at the end of last month.
Profit collapse, defaults, and bankruptcies
Sharp stock market crashes can have long-term consequences. For example, the Moscow Exchange Index returned to its pre-2008 crisis level of around 1,900 points only eight years later, while the RTS Index never returned to that level. In May–June 2008, Gazprom was worth around $340 billion and ranked third in the world by market capitalization, behind only ExxonMobil ($476 billion) and PetroChina ($441 billion).
In 2008, Gazprom was worth $340 billion, ranking third in the world and trailing only ExxonMobil and PetroChina
Today, Gazprom's valuation of $25-28 billion is well under 10% of its previous worth, and if measured in gold, it falls to less than 2% (if the company were valued in gold bars, it would have gone from being a large house full of the stuff to little more than a closet). ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil and gas corporation and the main surviving fragment of the Rockefeller empire, is now worth $650 billion – 36% more than it was 18 years ago. In 2008, Gazprom’s market capitalization was 71% of ExxonMobil’s; today, it is 4%. ExxonMobil is not even among the world’s 20 largest oil and gas companies; and yet, it is worth more than all Russian issuers combined.
Even within Russia, Gazprom has long since ceased to be the most valuable company, ranking only fifth – behind Sberbank, Rosneft, NOVATEK, and Lukoil. At the end of March, its shares traded at 138 rubles, but on July 17 they fell 42%, reaching an all-time low of 79 rubles (open trading of the company began only in 2006). The correction has brought it up to the 90-ruble range.
Rosneft shares fell almost as sharply: by 41% at the bottom and by 30% after the correction. NOVATEK performed slightly better, and Lukoil slightly better still. Nevertheless, losses across the entire oil and gas sector amounted to at least 20%. The decline in metals and mining was less severe, with the main sell-off occurring in 2024. And the decline in financial and technology stocks was more moderate.
The decline in Russian stock prices is linked to the overall decline in profits of Russian businesses. However, the stock market has moved much more sharply. The aggregate financial result of Russian organizations for January–May 2026 amounted to 99% of the previous year’s figure. Interestingly, the oil and gas sector, which saw the steepest decline in stock prices, recorded a 70% increase in profits compared with the previous year. This apparent contradiction can be explained by the fact that stock prices reflect not current conditions but market participants’ expectations. And those expectations incorporate the assumption that, given the sanctions and Ukrainian strikes on oil and gas processing and transportation infrastructure, the profitable period for oil and gas companies will not last long.
In the metals and mining sector, by contrast, profits fell six- to sevenfold, but stock prices did not fall nearly as sharply. This is because their share prices are already at very low levels compared with their prewar peak. The second round of declines in Russian metals producers’ share prices began in spring 2024. At the time, the United States and the United Kingdom banned imports of Russian-origin aluminum, copper, and nickel and also restricted their use on global metal exchanges and in derivatives trading.
Overall, the market remains near its lows even after the correction. A Moscow Exchange Index reading of around 2,300 corresponds to the worst point of the pandemic panic in 2020 and of the lowest levels seen during the war (from April 2022 to March 2023). An RTS Index below 900 points likewise matches levels seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and at the start of the war.
As stock prices fall, bond defaults are also being announced on an almost daily basis on the Moscow Exchange. There were 62 defaults in July (including technical defaults), a year-on-year six-fold increase. With borrowing costs high and business activity declining, issuers are finding it increasingly difficult to meet their debt obligations.
Business bankruptcies are also becoming more frequent. In the first half of 2026, there were 11% more of them than in the same period last year. The number of cases in which a company is placed under observation (the first stage of bankruptcy proceedings) increased by 21%. This process accelerated particularly sharply in April–June.
However, the number of bankruptcies has not yet reached their 2024 peak, which was driven by a trend towards tightening monetary policy That year, the Bank of Russia raised the key rate three from 16% to 21%. However, after entering 2026 back at that same 16% rate, the Central Bank has made further cuts, bringing it to 14%. The average RUONIA rate was 17.3% per annum in 2024, compared with 14.9% over the part of 2026 that has elapsed so far. Clearly, borrowing is now cheaper than it was in 2024, which is why there are still fewer bankruptcies.
The problems in the stock market in 2026, like the difficulties faced by the companies behind them, can easily be explained by monetary policy.
Stages of war grief
Since the start of the full-scale war, the Central Bank’s monetary-policy swings have gone through four stages.
Fear of inflation
In February 2022, at an emergency meeting held overnight on a Sunday, the Central Bank sharply raised the key rate from 9.5% to 20%, fearing rising prices. That fear was entirely justified. Year-on-year inflation subsequently jumped to 17–18%, according to official figures, and without the rate hike, things would have been even worse.
However, this stage did not last long. After all, in addition to inflation, the Russian economy was hit by the inevitable decline in production (and of business activity in general). In particular, foreign investors left the country en masse, while some found their funds frozen.
The stock market plunged sharply. Between February 25 and March 24, 2022, stock trading on the Moscow Exchange was suspended altogether. Once operations resumed, it became clear that a return to prewar stock prices and trading volumes was out of the question. At the end of April, the Moscow Exchange Index was 20% below its level on the eve of February 24. Under these circumstances, the Central Bank began to regard a depressed economic trajectory as the main danger.
Fear of recession
The second stage lasted from May 2022 to August 2023. During this period, the key rate was rapidly cut, holding at 7.5% for most of the period. The money supply grew from 68 trillion rubles to 90 trillion as the crisis was flooded with money.
The short-term consequences for the economy were exactly what had been hoped for: optimism took hold in a country at war. In April 2023, the Moscow Exchange Index returned to 2,500 points, reaching 3,000 in July. By the end of August, it was already at 3,200 – higher than on the eve of February 24, 2022!
Starting in the second quarter of 2023, Rosstat reported a return to GDP growth – at impressive rates of 4–5% year-on-year. Official inflation, responding with a lag to the anti-crisis measures, continued to decline through April 2023. Moreover, from March to June, it remained below the 4% target. However, it reached 4.3% in July and 5.1% in August. The attempt to bring it back to moderate levels failed.
Renewed fear of inflation
From July 2023 to October 2024, the Bank of Russia raised the key rate eight times, taking it to a record 21%, and then kept it at that level for nine months. At first, this did not help – the accumulated effects of the previous period of cheap money were too strong. And the expansion of the money supply did not stop, growing from 90 trillion to 119 trillion rubles.
Until July-August 2024, price growth continued to accelerate, reaching 9%, according to official figures. The stock market also did not perceive this policy as particularly tight, and through May-June 2024, the Moscow Exchange Index was broadly flat.
In the second half of 2024, monetary policy reached its maximum level of tightness: stocks plunged, while the number of bankruptcies reached a record high. The stock market suffered another major decline, partly as a result of sanctions against the Moscow Exchange.
However, rather than falling, inflation remained steady at around 9% a year until the very end of this stage. Under these circumstances, the Bank of Russia changed its priorities again without waiting for a clear and visible victory over inflation. In 2025, the decline in stock prices was accompanied by a sharp slowdown in GDP growth, to 1–1.3% a year. Once again, fears of an economic downturn came to the fore.
Renewed fear of recession
The Central Bank continues to say that “pro-inflationary risks outweigh disinflationary risks,” while systematically cutting the key rate. As always, the effects are not immediate.
Inflation through the end of 2025 was determined by the conditions of the preceding period of tight monetary policy, with price growth slowing to 6% year-on-year. In 2026, however, there has been no further slowdown: inflation has remained at around 6%. Moreover, the outlook is unfavorable. As recently as June, the Bank of Russia forecast that “annual inflation will decline to 4.5-5.5% in 2026.” By July 24, however, it had given a different forecast: “According to the Bank of Russia’s forecast, annual inflation will be 6–7% in 2026 due to the significant increase in fuel prices.”
Whether fuel is to blame or not, the Russian economy's situation is now critical both in terms of inflation and of real output. Inflation rose in response to the easing of monetary policy, and when that policy was then eased a little further, the inflation forecast was raised accordingly. Meanwhile, real GDP had already contracted in January and February, even according to Rosstat figures. Russian companies’ shares have been falling for the third year in a row, with the annual return negative in 2024, 2025, and in the part of 2026 that has elapsed so far.
The negative trend is being exacerbated by the growing erosion of property rights, as controlling stakes in various companies are increasingly being transferred from private owners to the state through legal actions that are becoming less and less transparent. A precedent was set by the nationalization of a controlling stake in the gold-mining company UGC, a process that harmed not only the majority shareholder accused of legal violations, but also minority shareholders, who did not receive the buyout offer required by law.
While the Central Bank can fully control inflation, it can influence the level of business activity only in the short term. Once the fundamental conditions for an economic downturn have taken hold in a country, no monetary policy can reverse them.
It should not be forgotten that war means diverting labor and capital away from productive activity and into destructive activity. It means death and injury for some people, emigration for others, and burnout and exhaustion for almost everyone. It means consuming accumulated reserves. It means replacing familiar and predictable rules with chaotic emergency measures – including nationalizations, price manipulation, and unpredictable seizures and giveaways worth trillions of rubles. It means isolation from the rest of the world, higher unit costs, direct physical destruction, and accelerated deterioration of infrastructure. It means environmental and social disasters from pollution to rising crime. Monetary “stimulus” is powerless in the face of such a calamity, and many economists believe that it is powerless even against regular cyclical crises.
Monetary “stimulus” is powerless in the face of the calamity of war and even regular cyclical crises
And yet, the second and fourth stages of the Bank of Russia’s wartime policy show precisely such attempts to stimulate the economy. At one point, they even created the illusion of an economic recovery (or at least softened the negative shock), but now they are close to exhausting their potential. Rather than preventing the inevitable economic downturn, they are merely postponing it while dooming the country to a state of stagflation – and since no central bank will ever care to acknowledge that it has created stagflation, once it comes within one step of it, it will again seek to tighten monetary conditions.
Russia is therefore now close to entering a fifth stage, when rate cuts will once again come to an end. The stock market will then fall even further, while bankruptcies, defaults, and losses will increase. Production statistics, and perhaps GDP as well, will show negative growth.
An anti-inflationary policy requires ruthlessness. The only question is whether Russia’s monetary authorities have a mandate from the Kremlin to pursue such a course. The last two times the Bank of Russia cut the key rate, the reductions were minimal – just 0.25 percentage points – and both times, the decisions were preceded by public statements from Vladimir Putin that the rate should be lowered.
However, the Central Bank stated in its new medium-term forecast that expected inflation was higher and GDP growth was lower than in its previous projection. It is as if the Central Bank is hinting that if Putin personally wants to control the key rate, then he should also explain the bad news to the public.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi military ship, four escort vessels in Red Sea
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they had attacked what they described as a Saudi military ship and four escort vessels in the Red Sea with missiles, according to a statement by the group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree on Telegram.
“The attack was carried out using several ballistic missiles, and the strikes were accurate and direct," the statement read.
"The operation resulted in the Saudi warship catching fire completely; several of the boats escorting it sank, while the others caught fire. The armed forces continue to establish the equation of blockade for blockade and to attack all Saudi military concentrations.”
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the attack.
Houthi attacks on 'Saudi-backed forces' in Mocha
Yemen's Mocha port, near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea has suspended commercial and maritime operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in Houthi attacks over recent days, the port's director said on Saturday.
The attacks killed seven people and caused an estimated $16 million in losses, the director told a news conference.
Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government control the port. It has a smaller cargo capacity than Yemen's main ports of Aden and Hodeidah.
Yemen's government said on Friday the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at Mocha that day, killing at least four civilians and targeting civilian, economic, and maritime facilities.
Following the attacks, the Houthis said they targeted a military build-up of weapons and warships belonging to Saudi-backed forces in Mocha.

articles.title: Ukraine Is Unleashing Flamingo Missiles on Russia at Nearly Twice the Pace of Six Months Ago
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Is Unleashing Flamingo Missiles on Russia at Nearly Twice the Pace of Six Months Ago
Ukraine is turning its homegrown Flamingo cruise missile from a rare deep-strike weapon into a recurring threat for Russia.
Ukraine has sharply increased its use of domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles against targets inside Russia this summer, with the pace of attacks nearly doubling over the past six months, Russian media outlet Agentstvo reported on August 15.
Russian media reached the conclusion after analyzing figures released by Russia’s Defense Ministry, which point to a significant increase in reported Flamingo launches since February.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Agentstvo, Russia’s Defense Ministry has claimed to have intercepted at least 57 Flamingo missiles since June. By comparison, Moscow reported 31 interceptions between February and May.
The reported pace has accelerated further in recent weeks. Russian authorities claimed that at least 25 Flamingo missiles were shot down in just the past two weeks.
Those figures are based on Russian military statements and do not necessarily reflect the actual number of missiles launched or intercepted.
At least four Flamingo strikes have been independently confirmed this summer, including attacks against facilities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The increase suggests that Ukraine is moving the Flamingo from a weapon used in relatively limited numbers toward a more regular role in its long-range strike campaign against Russian military and industrial targets.
The missile is domestically produced, giving Ukraine greater freedom to determine how and where it is used compared with some Western-supplied weapons that have previously come with restrictions on strikes inside Russia.
If the current launch tempo continues, the Flamingo could become an increasingly important element of Ukraine’s campaign to pressure Russia’s military infrastructure far beyond the front line.
In addition, Ukrainian Fire Point FP-1 drones struck Wildberries’ largest warehouse in Russia’s Moscow region, causing a large fire at the logistics complex in Koledino.
The company said the Koledino facility covers about 250,000 square meters and is used to store, sort, and distribute dual-use goods.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine sent 600 drones toward the Moscow region over 24 hours, the largest number recorded heading toward the Russian capital since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Russia builds and expands at least 10 drone bases. Some could put Warsaw in range – Telegraph
articles.body:
Russia has built or expanded at least 10 drone bases along its borders with Ukraine and Belarus, creating launch capacity for newer jet-powered attack drones, the most powerful of which could reach Warsaw, The Telegraph reported on 16 August 2026.
The network expands Russia’s capacity for mass drone attacks on Ukraine, while some sites could later threaten NATO. The findings come as Russia is also expanding bases and other military infrastructure along NATO’s northern and Baltic borders. The Telegraph found no evidence that Moscow is planning such an attack.
Seven of the 10 sites were used during recent bombardments of Kyiv, tracking data cited by The Telegraph showed. Using leaked documents, satellite imagery, and DroneSec's analysis, the newspaper identified at least 59 launch rails—tracks that launch fixed-wing drones without runways.
Around 20 appeared long enough for Russia’s latest long-range models, while one base could reportedly store over 1,000 drones.
Leaked Ukrainian documents cited by The Telegraph say the jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 can carry 90-kilogram warheads. However, Ukrainian military intelligence puts the Geran-4’s range at up to 450 kilometers, while the larger Geran-5 has a stated range of up to 1,000 kilometers — enough to reach Warsaw from several of the new sites.
DroneSec founder Mike Monnik said expanded launch capacity and harder-to-intercept technology together increase pressure on Ukrainian air defenses.
Russia builds military infrastructure along NATO’s northern flank
Russia is also expanding military infrastructure elsewhere along NATO’s borders. A Nordic-Baltic investigation identified new or expanded infrastructure from Norway to Kaliningrad, with potential capacity for up to 115,000 personnel.
Satellite imagery showed new barracks, ammunition warehouses, and expanded bases near NATO’s northern and Baltic members.
The Institute for the Study of War, a US-based think tank, assessed that the construction likely supports future Russian operations against NATO rather than an imminent attack. Most Russian combat power remains committed to Ukraine, it said.
Other drone hubs support rapid Russian attacks
Russia has already built comparable hubs for attacks on Ukraine. Satellite imagery analyzed by the open-source intelligence group Strategic Aviation of Russia showed 10 additional launchers under construction at Tsymbulova in Oryol Oblast, following the start of work on 22 April 2026.
At occupied Donetsk Airport, the group identified enlarged launch pads, roads to a Geran and Gerbera drone warehouse, and the apparent construction of another storage building.
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said it struck Shahed storage and launch sites at Primorsko-Akhtarsk on 2 August 2025. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi reported hitting drone logistics, warhead-storage, and preparation facilities at Donetsk Airport on 30 December 2025.

articles.title: Russia’s strikes across 10 Ukrainian regions kill at least eight in 24 hours
articles.body:
Russian forces shelled and struck front-line and border regions across northern, eastern, and southern Ukraine over the past 24 hours, killing at least eight civilians and wounding more than 40, regional authorities reported on 17 August. Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts reported deaths, while people were wounded in Kharkiv, Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk, Chernihiv, and Odesa Oblasts.
Russia's daily strikes have hit populated areas and civilian infrastructure both near the front line and far behind it. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 13 regions had come under attack over the past week, with more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles, most of them ballistic, launched at Ukraine.
North: FPV drone attacks firefighters’ vehicle
In Sumy Oblast, Russian forces carried out more than 50 strikes on 24 settlements across 11 communities. A drone strike in the Sumy community killed a 75-year-old man and a 72-year-old woman and wounded another civilian, the Sumy military administration said. It also said two more people were wounded in the Seredyna-Buda community. A mass drone attack on Sumy caused large fires and wounded at least one person, Sumy city military administration head Serhii Kryvosheienko said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, a 41-year-old man was wounded in a Geran drone strike on the Kozelets community, Head of the Regional Military Administration Viacheslav Chaus said. He added that Gerbera drones destroyed a hangar and farm equipment in the Kholmy community. In a border village in the Horodnia community, an FPV drone struck a yard, and a second FPV drone hit a firefighters' vehicle that had arrived at the scene. A house later caught fire. A critical infrastructure facility was also hit.
In Kharkiv Oblast, six people were wounded in strikes on Kharkiv and nine other settlements. The heaviest damage was reported in Izium, where 19 houses and four apartment blocks were damaged, head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov said.
East: Russian strikes destroy 30 stalls
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces killed two residents of Kramatorsk and wounded 18 people across the region, Head of the Regional Military Administration Vadym Filashkin said. In Sloviansk, round-the-clock strikes damaged critical infrastructure and destroyed 30 stalls at the Lisnyi market, Sloviansk City Military Administration Head Vadym Liakh said.
  In Poltava Oblast, two industrial facilities were hit, causing fires, and drones also attacked another industrial facility in Myrhorod district, Head of the Regional Military Administration Vitalii Diakivnych said. No casualties were reported.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian forces attacked four districts nearly 20 times from the evening of 16 August, wounding five people, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that houses and outbuildings caught fire in Pavlohrad and Nikopol district.
In Zaporizhzhia district, two people were killed and three wounded, Head of the Regional Military Administration Ivan Fedorov said. He also reported 1,217 strikes on 60 settlements across the oblast, including 20 air strikes, about 846 drone attacks, and 350 artillery strikes.
South: strike damages civilian vessel flying the flag of Togo
In Odesa Oblast, a night-time strike on port infrastructure damaged a civilian vessel flying the flag of Togo and wounded four people, one of them seriously, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Kiper said.
In Kherson Oblast, in the early morning, Russian forces killed two residents of the village of Novokayiry in the Mylivska community, – Head of the Kherson Regional State Administration Oleksandr Prokhudin said. Also russian forces attacked 52 settlements, including the regional capital. Six people were wounded, while 11 apartment blocks and 15 private houses were damaged, Prokudin said.
In Mykolaiv Oblast, Russia attacked with Shahed and Gerbera drones, but no casualties were reported, acting Head of the Regional Military Administration Heorhii Reshetilov said. He added that the roof of an agricultural enterprise building was damaged in the Horokhivska community.
